passages.title: Praise to the Creator of light and darkness
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah al-Anʿām 1–3 — Praise to the Creator of light and darkness

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up these three verses as a sequence. The first verse tells us about the "big universe" — the whole wide world of heavens, earth, darkness and light — created and made by Allah. The second verse turns to the "small universe," the human being: your origin from clay and the two appointed ends awaiting you. The third verse then contains what Maʿārif calls the consequential outcome of the first two: the One who made both universes is the only Being worthy of worship and obedience in all the heavens and the earth, and He knows everything human beings conceal or reveal.

## A sūrah that came down with seventy thousand angels

Ibn Kathir opens his commentary with the sūrah's remarkable pedigree. Al-ʿAwfi, ʿIkrimah and ʿAtaʾ said that Ibn ʿAbbas said, "Sūrat al-Anʿām was revealed in Makkah." At-Tabarani recorded that Ibn ʿAbbas said, "All of Sūrat al-Anʿām was revealed in Makkah at night, accompanied by seventy thousand angels, raising their voices in glorification of Allah." And as-Suddi said that Murrah said that ʿAbdullah said, "Sūrat al-Anʿām was revealed in the company of seventy thousand angels."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas that one of the distinctions of this sūrah is that the whole of it, except some āyāt, was revealed at one time in Makkah, with a complement of seventy thousand angels following it with recitation of the name of Allah — and that early tafsir authorities such as Mujahid, al-Kalbi and Qatadah said more or less the same thing. Maʿārif also cites Abu Ishaq al-Asfraʾini's summary of the sūrah's substance: it consists of all the principles and subsidiaries of Tawhid — the Oneness of Allah. These first three verses are that Tawhid in concentrated form.

## "All praise is for Allah" — and the proof follows immediately

The sūrah is prefaced with *al-hamdu lillāh*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the perspective this is meant to give us: Allah does not need our praise. Whether or not anyone praises Him, He is, in terms of His own intrinsic perfection, by Himself, the Praised One. What the verse does is supply the *proof* in the very next breath: He "created the heavens and the earth, and made the darkness and the light." Would not the Being who holds such Power and Wisdom have to be the One deserving of all praise?

Ibn Kathir reads the same verse with warmth: Allah praises His Most Honorable Self for creating the heavens and earth *as a dwelling for His servants*, and for making the darkness and light *to benefit them* in the night and the day. The universe is not merely evidence; it is a kindness.

## Four deliberate choices of wording

The Arabic of ayah 1 is precise in ways an English translation flattens, and both commentaries linger over it.

**"Created" versus "made."** The heavens and earth are *khalaqa* — created — while darkness and light are *jaʿala* — made, originated. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sees a hint here: darkness and light are not independent, self-existent things like the heavens and the earth; they are contingents and attributes — they exist only in dependence on other things.

**"Darknesses" plural, "light" singular.** The Arabic says *zulumāt* — layers of darkness, plural — but *an-nūr*, the light, singular. Ibn Kathir explains that the light is given the singular "because an-Nūr is more honored," and points to the same pattern elsewhere: "To the right and to the lefts" (16:48), and near the end of this very sūrah, "this is my straight path, so follow it, and follow no (other) ways, for they will separate you away from His way" (6:153) — one path, many ways. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Mazhari and al-Bahr al-Muhit) makes the symbolism explicit: light signifies the correct way, the straight path — and that is just one; the darknesses signify the path of error — and their number runs in thousands.

**"Heavens" plural, "earth" singular.** Though another verse (65:12) identifies the earths as being seven like the heavens, the earth here is singular. Mazhari's suggestion, relayed in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: the seven heavens are mutually distinct in form and attributes, while the seven earths are like each other, and so were taken as one in number.

**Darkness before light.** Why mention *zulumāt* first? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān suggests it is because darkness is basic to this world, while light is associated with particulars — when they are there, there is light, and when they are not, there is darkness.

## "Yet those who disbelieve hold others as equal with their Lord"

Then comes the sting at the end of ayah 1: *thumma* — "yet," after all this. Ibn Kathir: in spite of all this, some of Allah's servants disbelieve in Him and hold others as partners and rivals with Him; some even claimed a wife and a son for Allah — hallowed be He far above what they attribute to Him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān shows just how wide a net this one clause casts — the verse points to the reality of Tawhid and its open proof in order to warn all those peoples who either do not believe in Tawhid at all, or have forsaken its reality despite professing it. The Magians (Majūs) believed in two creators — Yazdan, creator of good, and Ahriman, creator of evil — and identified them with light and darkness. The polytheists of India took an incredibly high number of partners in divinity; the Arya Samajists, despite acknowledging Tawhid, held spirit and matter to be infinitely pre-existent and independent of Allah's power and creation; and the Christians, despite professing the creed of Tawhid, took ʿIsa (peace be upon him) and his blessed mother as partners in divinity, propping the belief up with the theory of "Unity in Trinity." As for the polytheists of Arabia, they went so far that any piece of rock on a hill could become an object of worship — not just the moon, the sun and the stars, but fire, water, trees, rocks, even crawling insects, taken as objects of prostration and worship, providers of needs and resolvers of problems. By declaring that Allah is the Creator of the heavens and the earth and the Maker of darkness and light, Maʿārif says, all such false notions stand refuted — when He is the sole Creator and Maker of everything, ascribing partners to His divinity makes no sense.

## The small universe: you, from clay (ayah 2)

Having shown Allah's hand in the vast world, the passage turns to the world you know most intimately — yourself. "He it is Who has created you from clay." Ibn Kathir says this refers to Adam, the father of mankind, from whom humanity originated, multiplied in numbers and spread about, east and west. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the ongoing chain: Allah created Adam (peace be upon him) with clay and then gave him life — and common human food comes from the moist substance of clay, from food comes the sperm, and from the sperm comes the creation of the human being.

The commentary records a hadith here: Abu Musa al-Ashʿari said he heard the Prophet ﷺ say that Allah created Adam from a particular blend of clay containing essential ingredients of the whole earth — and this is why the children of Adam differ in colour, shape, morals and habits: some black or white or red, some hard or soft, good-natured or evil-tempered. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites this through Mazhari, from a narration of Ibn ʿAdiyy, described as being of good authority. Human diversity, on this reading, is written into our very substance.

## The two appointed terms

"Then He decreed a term (*ajal*), and a determined term is with Him." What are the two terms? Ibn Kathir records a genuine difference among the early commentators:

- **The first term is death; the second is the Hereafter.** This is the view of Saʿid bin Jubayr reporting from Ibn ʿAbbas, and similar statements were narrated from Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, Saʿid bin Jubayr, al-Hasan, Qatadah, ad-Dahhak, Zayd bin Aslam, ʿAtiyyah, as-Suddi, Muqatil bin Hayyan and others.
- **The first term is the span of this earthly life; the second is each person's extent of life until death.** Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid said this, connected to 6:60, where Allah takes souls by night in sleep and raises them again "that a term appointed (life) be fulfilled."

On either reading, the phrase "with Him" (*ʿindahu*) carries the same weight: none but Allah knows when that term will occur. Ibn Kathir supports this with 7:187 — "The knowledge thereof is with my Lord. None can reveal its time but He" — and 79:42–44: "They ask you about the Hour — when will be its appointed time? You have no knowledge to say anything about it. To your Lord belongs (the knowledge of) the term thereof."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān builds the argument on the first reading. Your personal end — death — is destined; reaching the completion of your term *is* death. You do not know its date (though, Maʿārif notes, the angels do), yet you can hardly doubt the fact of it: "incidents of the children of Adam dying all around, everywhere, all the time, are common experience." The second term is the combined end of the entire humankind along with all the cosmic servants waiting on them — the Qiyāmah, the Day of Doom — and *its* full knowledge has been given to no angel and no human being at all; it is known to Allah alone.

## "Yet you doubt"

The verse ends: *thumma antum tamtarūn* — "yet you doubt." Doubt what? As-Suddi says: the coming of the (last) Hour. And here Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the point the verse is making. You watch the small ending — death — overtake everyone around you, constantly, without exception. Using that observed, personal death as proof of the general, collective death of the whole world-system is, in Maʿārif's words, "something very natural and logical." So the verse does not merely inform; it *wonders* — why would people keep doubting the coming of the Qiyāmah when it stands proved so clearly? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says this is said "to shake human beings out of their negligence": every human being has a particular age, after which death is certain.

## Ayah 3: the conclusion — He is Allah in the heavens and the earth

"And He is Allah in the heavens and in the earth." Ibn Kathir explains this phrase with care: it means that it is *He* Who is called Allah throughout the heavens and the earth — He Who is worshipped and singled out, Whose divinity the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth believe in. They call Him Allah and supplicate to Him in fear and hope — except those who disbelieve among the jinn and mankind. He compares another ayah, rendered in the commentary as "It is He Who is God in the heavens and the earth" (43:84) — meaning, Ibn Kathir says, He is the God of those in heaven and those on earth, and He knows all affairs, public and secret.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this verse "the consequential outcome" of the first two: since He alone made the great universe and the small one, He alone is the Being worthy of worship and obedience in all the heavens and the earth.

And the passage closes on His knowledge: "He knows what you conceal and what you reveal, and He knows what you earn." Ibn Kathir: He knows all affairs, public and secret — and "what you earn" means all the good and bad deeds that you perform. Notice how the three verses have moved: ayah 1 established who He is and why He is praised; ayah 2 established where you came from and where you are going; ayah 3 establishes that the whole journey between those two points is fully seen. Your secret and your public speech are equally known to Him, and your deeds are not merely actions but *earnings* — all the good and bad you perform, gathered and known.

## What the passage asks of you

The passage's own demands are simple and severe. Praise belongs to Allah alone — and since He is the sole Creator and Maker of everything, ascribing any partner to His divinity, whether light or darkness, star or stone, makes no sense. Your death is decreed and its term rests with Him — so let the constant sight of death around you cure your doubt about the Qiyāmah to come, rather than leaving you in the negligence this verse was sent to shake off. And since He knows your concealed and your revealed alike, let the inner life be as clean as the outer one — for both are being earned.

passages.title: The deniers turn away from every sign
passages.tafsir:
This passage is a portrait of denial — not the denial of someone who has not yet seen enough evidence, but the denial of someone who has decided in advance not to believe. Ayat 4–5 state the disease: every sign that comes, they turn away from. Ayat 6 and 11 frame the passage with its cure and its warning: look at history, at the ruined nations before you. And ayat 7–10 take us inside actual conversations in Makkah, where the idolators made hostile demands for miracles — a book floating down on paper, an angel standing beside the Prophet ﷺ — and Allah exposes what those demands really were, then turns to comfort His Messenger ﷺ.

## A settled refusal, not an honest doubt

In ayah 4, Allah says that no *āyah* — the word means a sign, and covers a verse of revelation, a miracle, or any proof — comes to these people from their Lord except that they turn away from it. Ibn Kathir notes the force of this: the rebellious, stubborn polytheists turn away from *every* sign of Allah's Uniqueness and of the truth of His Messengers, without contemplating them or caring about them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls it a complaint against the "anti-truth doggedness" of the heedless: whatever sign is shown for their guidance, they have a settled way of averting their faces from it. The problem is not the evidence; it is the posture.

Ayah 5 then names what they rejected: *al-ḥaqq*, "the truth." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a striking observation here — *al-ḥaqq* can mean the Qur'an, and it can equally mean the blessed person of the Prophet ﷺ himself. Why? Because he was himself a walking proof. He had lived his entire life before their eyes — child, young man, mature adult. All of Arabia knew him as *ummiyy*, unlettered: he had never studied under any teacher, could not so much as write his own name, and showed no interest in poetry, the prized art of the age. Then, after forty years, came a sudden, unimaginable flowering: his tongue became a fountainhead of insight and knowledge that disarmed the best minds of the world. He openly challenged every master of Arabic eloquence to produce even one ayah like the Qur'an's — and his enemies, who would have sacrificed life, wealth, honour and family to defeat him, could not accept the challenge. The man they had watched for forty years *was* the sign. To reject him was to reject the truth standing in front of them.

The ayah closes with a warning wrapped in restraint: "there will come to them the news of what they used to mock at." They laughed at the idea of Qiyāmah (the Day of Rising) and the Ākhirah (the Hereafter); soon, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, those realities will be before their eyes — a real Reckoning, real reward and punishment. But believing *then* will not help, because that Day is not a day of deeds but of retribution. The time to think is now: the respite Allah has given is, in Maʿārif's phrase, a God-sent piece of luck. Ibn Kathir reads the same words as a stern threat: the deniers will surely know the truth of what they denied and taste the evil end of their behaviour.

## The lesson written in ruins (ayah 6)

Ayah 6 asks: "Have they not *seen* how many a generation before them We destroyed?" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that "seen" here means *pondered* — those generations were not physically there to look at. The word for "generation," *qarn*, deserves attention: it means a people living together in one age, and it is also used for a long stretch of time — between ten and a hundred years, on different interpretations. Maʿārif cites reports supporting the meaning of a hundred years: in one hadith the Prophet ﷺ told ʿAbdullah ibn Busr al-Māzinī that he would live for one *qarn*; and on another occasion, when the Prophet ﷺ prayed for a certain child that he might live a whole *qarn*, that child lived a full hundred years. The majority of scholars understand the famous saying "the best of generations is my generation, then those who follow them, then those who follow them" — still recited in the Friday sermon across the world — in this sense, each *qarn* being a hundred years.

Allah describes what those vanished peoples had: He established them on the earth as He has *not* established you, poured abundant rain on them, and made rivers flow beneath them. Ibn Kathir spells it out — more wealth, children, buildings, provision and soldiers than these addressees ever possessed. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the comparison for the direct audience: the people of Makkah had neither the power of the legendary ʿĀd and Thamūd nor the affluence of the peoples of Syria and Yemen. Yet when those far greater nations belied their prophets, all that majesty proved useless: "We destroyed them for their sins." And then — a detail both commentaries dwell on — "We created after them other generations." Divine power did not merely level the mighty; it raised new peoples on the very ashes of the old, as if no one were missing from the scene. The author of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān recalls standing at ʿArafāt among a million men and women and realising that a mere seventy or eighty years earlier, not one of them existed — while nearly that many other human beings had stood on that same plain, of whom no trace remained.

Ibn Kathir draws the warning to its sharpest point: beware the same end, for you are not dearer to Allah than those previous nations were — but the Messenger you are defying is dearer to Allah than the messengers they defied. If anything, that makes the defiant *more* liable to punishment, were it not for Allah's mercy and kindness. Maʿārif adds why the Qur'an tells history this way: past events, pondered rightly, are more effective than a thousand sermons — as the saying of the sage he quotes has it, the world is the best book, and time the best teacher. The Qur'an never narrates history as entertainment or an end in itself; it gives each fragment where the lesson belongs, because the point is not the story but what you do with it.

## The demands behind ayat 7–9: scenes from Makkah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the occasion behind ayah 7. ʿAbdullah ibn Abi Umayyah confronted the Prophet ﷺ with a hostile demand: "I cannot believe in you until I see you climb all the way to the heavens and bring down a book, before our eyes, with my name written in it telling me to attest to your prophethood" — and then added that even if all this happened, he still did not expect to be impressed enough to convert. The demand was designed to be unmeetable and was announced, in advance, as pointless. (Strange are the ways of fate, Maʿārif observes: this same man later embraced Islam with such fervour that he died a martyr at the Battle of Ṭā'if.)

Ayah 7 answers the demand by granting it hypothetically and pushing it further: even if Allah sent down a book written on *qirṭās* — paper, a physical page — and they not only watched it descend but *touched it with their own hands* to rule out any trick of the eye, they would still say, "This is nothing but obvious magic." Ibn Kathir links this to a pattern the Qur'an describes elsewhere: if a gate were opened for them into heaven and they kept ascending through it, they would say "our eyes have been dazzled; we are a people bewitched" (15:14–15); if they saw a piece of the sky falling, they would call it "clouds heaped up" (52:44). The problem was never the evidence. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names the real source of the objection: what they say comes from malice and hostility.

Ayah 8 has its own occasion: the same ʿAbdullah ibn Abi Umayyah returned, this time with Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith and Nawfal ibn Khālid, demanding that the Prophet ﷺ bring a book from the heavens accompanied by four angels testifying to it. Allah's reply — "Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been judged at once, and no respite would be granted them" — rests on a divine law Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains: when a people demand a miracle of their own choosing, and Allah grants it, and they *still* refuse to believe, they are destroyed by a general punishment, with no further respite. Ibn Kathir cites the parallel: "We send not the angels down except with the truth, and in that case they would have no respite" (15:8), and "On the Day they see the angels, no glad tidings will there be for the criminals that day" (25:22). These Makkans were not asking in good faith; granting their demand would simply have sealed their doom. So the withholding of the spectacular miracle was not evasion — as Maʿārif puts it, it spelled out real good for them. The unanswered demand was the very thing keeping them alive.

Ayah 9 gives a second answer, this one about the nature of the request itself. An angel can come in only two ways. In his true form — and, says Maʿārif, no human being could stand before that awe; one is more likely to die at the never-imagined sight. Ibn Kathir relates through aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk that Ibn ʿAbbās said an angel sent to them would have to come in the shape of a man, "because they will not be able to look at the angel due to light." Or the angel comes in human form, as Jibrīl (peace be upon him) came to the Prophet ﷺ many times — in which case the objector is back exactly where he started, facing someone who looks like an ordinary man, and, says Maʿārif, he would raise against this "angel" the very objection he raises against the Prophet ﷺ. Hence the ayah's ending: "We would have certainly caused them confusion in the matter they have already covered with confusion" — or, in another report of Ibn ʿAbbās cited by Ibn Kathir through al-Wālibī, "We brought doubts around them." Their demand, granted, would only multiply their own muddle.

Ibn Kathir closes this discussion with the positive truth underneath it: it is a *mercy* from Allah that He sends to every kind of creation messengers from their own kind, so that people can speak with their messenger, question him, and benefit from him — "If there were on the earth angels walking about in peace, We would have sent down to them from heaven an angel as a messenger" (17:95); "Indeed Allah conferred a great favour on the believers when He sent among them a Messenger from among themselves" (3:164). The Prophet's ﷺ humanity, which his opponents treated as a disqualification, was precisely the point.

## Comfort for the one who carried the message (ayat 10–11)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses over something easy to miss: what did these mocking, insulting exchanges do to the Prophet's ﷺ heart? He was more affectionate toward his people than their own parents could be — and they answered him with caustic contempt. We cannot fathom the wound; only someone consumed with the good of his people as he was could sense it.

Ayah 10 is Allah's consolation. Messengers before him were mocked in just this way — this pain is not unique to him, and those earlier prophets did not lose hope. And the end of the story is fixed: "their scoffers were surrounded by the very thing they used to mock at." The punishment they laughed at closed in around them. Ibn Kathir reads in this both comfort for the Messenger ﷺ and a promise, to him and to the believers, of Allah's victory and the good end in this life and the Hereafter. Maʿārif draws out the lesson Allah taught him: his mission is to *convey*. Once he has done that, let his heart be at rest — whether anyone is moved by the message is not part of his duty, and it must bring no sorrow to his heart.

Then ayah 11 turns back to the deniers with a command that is really an invitation: "Say: travel through the land, then see what was the end of the deniers." Ibn Kathir explains: contemplate your own situation in the light of what struck the nations who defied and denied their messengers — torment in this life and painful torment in the Hereafter — while Allah saved His messengers and His believing servants. The passage thus ends where ayah 6 began: history itself is the standing sign, for whoever will ponder it.

## Living it

Two threads run through the whole passage for the believer. First, honesty about evidence: ayat 7–9 teach that a heart set on refusal will explain away *anything* — even a page touched with one's own hands — so the real question is never "is there enough proof?" but "am I willing?" The respite we live in is, in Maʿārif's phrase, "a God-sent piece of luck"; the time to act is now, for the Day of Reckoning is a day of retribution, not of deeds. Second, steadiness in conveying truth: ayah 10 teaches that mockery is the old tax on carrying Allah's message, that earlier messengers bore it without losing hope, and that our duty ends at faithful conveyance — the results belong to Allah.

passages.title: Say-commands proclaiming Allah's ownership and mercy
passages.tafsir:
**This passage is a volley of proclamations.** Again and again across these seven ayat the command *qul* — "Say!" — is placed on the tongue of the Prophet ﷺ, each declaration answering the idolaters of Makkah from a different angle. What holds the ayat together is one sustained argument: everything in existence belongs to Allah alone, so He alone is to be taken as protector, feared, and relied upon — and, astonishingly, the Owner of everything has bound Himself to mercy. Majesty and tenderness run side by side from the first ayah ("He has prescribed mercy for Himself") to the last ("He is the All-Wise, the All-Aware").

## The question that answers itself (ayah 12)

"Ask them: to whom belongs everything in the heavens and the earth?" — and then, without waiting for a reply: "Say: to Allah." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why Allah supplies the answer Himself: it was a fact the questioners already conceded. The Makkans, for all their shirk and idolatry, never denied that Allah Almighty was Master of the heavens and the earth. The ayah simply makes them face their own admission — you already know who owns everything, so the case for worshipping Him alone is over before it begins.

Then comes one of the most consoling sentences in the Qur'an: *kataba ʿalā nafsihi al-raḥmah* — "He has prescribed mercy for Himself." No one obliged Him; He obliged Himself. Ibn Kathir grounds this in the hadith recorded in the Two Sahihs, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "When Allah created the creation, He wrote in a Book that He has with Him above the Throne: My mercy overcomes My anger."

The same ayah then turns to the Day of Resurrection — Ibn Kathir notes that Allah here swears by His own Most Honored Self that He will gather His servants to that Day, "about which there is no doubt." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing al-Qurtubi) draws attention to the little word *ilā*, "towards" that Day: it may mean He will gather every generation, first to last, together on the Day itself; or that humanity keeps being gathered into the graves until that Day comes and they are raised. Either way the destination is the same.

And the ayah closes: "those who have lost themselves — they will not believe." Maʿārif (again from al-Qurtubi) draws out the precision here: the disbelievers' exclusion from the universal mercy just mentioned was caused by their own deeds. Mercy was prescribed; they simply refused the road that leads to it — the road of faith.

## Whatever rests in the night and the day (ayah 13)

Ayah 12 spoke of ownership across space — the heavens and the earth. Ayah 13 adds ownership across time: "To Him belongs whatever rests (*sakana*) in the night and the day." The word *sakana* literally means to be still, at rest, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two readings: it may simply mean everything present in the night and day; or it may deliberately name only what is still and let what moves be understood — "what tarries and what stirs" — since movement, the obvious opposite, needs no mention. Nothing in either state falls outside His dominion. And He is *al-Samīʿ al-ʿAlīm* — as Ibn Kathir puts it, He hears the statements of His servants and knows their actions, their secrets, and what they conceal.

## The One who feeds and is never fed (ayah 14)

Now the argument becomes personal. The Prophet ﷺ is commanded: "Say: shall I take as a *walī* — a guardian, protector, patron — any other than Allah?" Ibn Kathir explains that the question is a refusal: I will take no guardian except Allah, without partners. And the ayah gives two reasons.

First, He is *Fāṭir* of the heavens and the earth — Ibn Kathir glosses this as the One who originated them without precedent.

Second, "it is He Who feeds and is not fed." He sustains His creatures without needing them — Ibn Kathir connects this to "I created not the jinn and humans except that they should worship Me" (51:56). He also notes that some scholars read the phrase as "He feeds but does not eat" — meaning, Allah does not eat. Ibn Kathir then relates the narration of Abu Hurayrah: a man of the Ansar from Quba invited the Prophet ﷺ to a meal, and when he had eaten and washed his hands he said, "All praise is due to Allah, Who feeds but is never fed… All thanks and praises are due to Allah Who fed us the food, gave us the drink, covered our nudity, guided us from misguidance, gave us sight from blindness, and honored us above many of His creatures. All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all that exists." The ayah's theology became the Prophet's ﷺ table manners.

Then: "I am commanded to be the first of those who submit" — the first, Ibn Kathir says, of this Ummah. The caller must be the first to answer his own call.

## "If I disobey my Lord" — even the Prophet ﷺ (ayat 15–16)

Ayah 15 is startling: the Prophet ﷺ himself is made to say, "I fear, if I were to disobey my Lord, the torment of a Mighty Day." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān addresses the obvious question head-on: the noble Messenger of Allah ﷺ is divinely protected from every sin, so the likelihood of disobedience from him simply does not exist. The hypothetical is stated for the community's sake, and Maʿārif calls its manner "particularly endearing": disobeying Allah is so serious a matter that even the greatest prophet ﷺ could not stand excused from its consequences — and if not him, who else?

Ayah 16 then shows mercy from an unexpected side. "Whoever is spared the torment of that Day — He has certainly been merciful to him." Maʿārif explains: the punishment of the Day of Gathering is so horrendous that merely to be spared it is itself a great mercy from Allah. "And that is the clear success (*al-fawz al-mubīn*)" — *fawz* here means admission into Paradise, and Maʿārif notes the wording teaches that deliverance from punishment and entry into Paradise are inseparable: whoever receives the one receives the other. Ibn Kathir hears the echo of 3:185 — "Whoever is moved away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has indeed succeeded" — success meaning pure gain with all loss negated.

Notice the quiet symmetry: ayah 12 announced that mercy is prescribed; ayah 16 shows what that mercy finally looks like — a person standing on the Day of Judgement while the torment is turned away from him.

## All harm and all good are in one hand (ayah 17)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls ayah 17 the statement of a cardinal article of Muslim faith: it is Allah, in reality, who is the Master-Dispenser of all gain and loss. No created being can truly bring the least benefit or cause the least harm; when help or hurt seems to come from people, that is appearance only — in Maʿārif's image, a curtain ready to vanish. He illustrates it with a Persian couplet: the fragrance is really the work of the beloved's tresses, yet the lovers find it expedient to blame the musk-deer of China — the apparent cause is credited with what belongs to another. And he calls this one of the revolutionary beliefs of Islam: it made Muslims shed dependence on the created and rely on their Creator alone, producing people who, despite meager means and haunting hunger, would bow their heads before no one.

Ibn Kathir sets beside this ayah its twin in Surah Fatir: "Whatever mercy Allah may grant to mankind, none can withhold it; and whatever He may withhold, none can grant it thereafter" (35:2) — and the supplication recorded in the Sahih that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to make: "O Allah, there is none who can avert what You grant or give what You deprive, and no fortune ever helps the fortunate against You."

Maʿārif adds the famous counsel al-Baghawi reports from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas, who rode behind the Prophet ﷺ and was told: "Remember Allah and Allah will remember you… When you have to ask, ask only Allah; when you need help, seek help only from Allah. If all of creation combined to bring you a benefit Allah has not written for you, they could never do it; and if they all combined to inflict on you a harm not in your lot, they could never do it… And know that the help of Allah is with patience, comfort with hardship, and prosperity with adversity." The bundle notes this hadith also appears in Tirmidhi and the Musnad of Ahmad with sound chains of authority.

**Living it.** Maʿārif closes with a pointed warning for our own time: many Muslims, in their hour of distress, cry out in all sorts of names rather than calling on Allah. Calling directly upon a created being for the removal of one's need, he says, is open rebellion against this Qur'anic injunction — though he distinguishes this from supplicating Allah Himself through the mediation of prophets and the righteous, which he holds permissible. The plain practice this ayah asks of a believer is the one the Prophet ﷺ taught the young Ibn ʿAbbas: when you ask, ask Allah.

## Al-Qāhir — supreme above His servants (ayah 18)

The passage seals its argument with three names. He is *al-Qāhir* — rendered by the commentators as the Irresistible, the Dominant — "above His servants" (*fawqa ʿibādih*). Ibn Kathir unfolds the name: to Him all necks are subservient, before Him the tyrants are humbled, and every creature stands under His irresistible decision and power. Maʿārif draws the everyday proof: His mastery prevails over His servants in the absolute sense — everyone remains under His power and control all the time — which is why no human being, however great, not a prophet close to Allah, not the most powerful ruler on earth, succeeds in everything he attempts or has every wish granted.

But raw power is not the final word. He is *al-Ḥakīm*, the All-Wise — everything He does, Maʿārif says, is essential wisdom — and *al-Khabīr*, the All-Aware, who knows everything; Ibn Kathir adds that He places everything in its rightful place and favors whoever deserves His favor. Maʿārif concludes that these names together declare that perfection in knowledge and power belongs to Allah alone — which is exactly why the passage began by asking whose the universe is, and why He alone deserves the trust, the fear, and the hope these ayat demand.

passages.title: Allah's supreme testimony and the idolaters' collapse
passages.tafsir:
This passage is a single courtroom drama played out twice. In ayah 19 the idolaters of Makkah demand a witness to Muhammad's ﷺ prophethood, and the answer given is Allah Himself — the greatest of all witnesses; by ayat 22–24 the idolaters are standing in the real courtroom of the Day of Resurrection, where the only testimony they can produce is a false oath — and even that collapses around them. What holds the six ayat together is the language of witness (*shahādah*): who testifies for the Prophet ﷺ, who dares testify against Allah, and whose testimony will still be standing on the Last Day.

## "Who is the greatest witness?" — the challenge behind ayah 19

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān records the occasion generally reported by the commentators. A deputation of the people of Makkah came to the Prophet ﷺ and said, in effect: *You claim to be a Messenger of Allah. Who is your witness? We have tried our best to confirm it from the Jews and Christians, and we have yet to see a man who attests to its truth.* Ayah 19 came in answer: whose witness could possibly be greater than that of Allah, in whose power lies every person's gain and loss? The "witness of Allah" here, Maʿārif explains, refers to the miracles and signs Allah made manifest to confirm the truth of His Prophet's ﷺ mission.

Ibn Kathir adds an intimate dimension to "Allah is Witness between me and you": He knows exactly what I have brought you, *and what you will answer me with*.

The same ayah then turns the question back on them: "Can you really bear witness that besides Allah there are other gods?" The Prophet ﷺ is commanded to answer for himself: "I bear no such witness… He is only One God, and I am innocent of what you associate with Him." Ibn Kathir notes the parallel command in 6:150 — *"then if they testify, testify not you with them."* Maʿārif adds the edge in the wording: even after Allah's own testimony, do you stand to witness *against Him*? If so, you are responsible for your own fate.

## "…and whomever it may reach"

Tucked into ayah 19 is one of the most far-reaching phrases in the surah: this Qur'an was revealed "that I may warn you with it — and whomever it may reach." Ibn Kathir: the Qur'an is a warner for everyone who hears of it, pairing it with 11:17, *"but those of the sects that reject it, the Fire will be their promised meeting place."* Ar-Rabiʿ bin Anas drew the practical conclusion: those who follow the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ought to call to what he called to and warn against what he warned against.

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān draws out two large truths from this phrase. First, it proves that the Prophet ﷺ is the Last Prophet and that the Qur'an will keep reaching people — recited and taught — right through to the Day of Qiyāmah, with people obliged to follow it. Second, reach creates responsibility. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: whomever the Qur'an has reached has become like one who has actually visited Muhammad ﷺ; and in another report, "To whomever the Qur'an has reached, I am his warner." This is why the Prophet ﷺ so emphatically told his Companions to convey his teachings "even if it be one ayah," and why — as ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd reports — he prayed that Allah keep hale and hearty the person who hears a saying of his, commits it to memory, and conveys it to his Ummah. Maʿārif adds a lovely observation on why conveying matters even when you don't fully understand: a person of a later time may grasp what the first hearer never appreciated.

## "As they recognize their own sons" (ayah 20)

Ayah 20 directly demolishes the Makkans' claim that the Jews and Christians would not vouch for him. On the contrary: "those to whom We gave the Scripture recognize him as they recognize their own children." Both commentators explain why. The Torah and the Injīl contained a full description of the Prophet ﷺ — his physical features, his home city and then his post-emigration place of residence, his habits, morals and achievements — in such detail, Maʿārif says, that it left no room for doubt; the earlier scriptures even carried descriptions of his noble Companions.

Maʿārif then lingers on the simile itself, and it repays the attention. The Qur'an says they know him *as they know their sons* — not "as children know their parents." Why? Because a parent's recognition of a child is the most detailed and certain recognition there is: from infancy the child is raised in the parents' hands and laps, before their eyes day and night. Children can never know their parents to that degree.

Two Companions from the People of the Book confirm this from the inside. When ʿUmar al-Fārūq asked ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām — a former Jew — about this ayah, he answered: yes, we know the Prophet ﷺ from the qualities and features Allah revealed in the Torah, so this knowledge of ours is certain and absolute — *unlike our own offspring, about whom one could doubt whether they are really ours.* And Zayd ibn Saʿnah, also formerly of the People of the Book, recognized the Prophet ﷺ from the Torah and Injīl descriptions except for a single quality he could only confirm by testing: "his forbearance will dominate his anger." He went, tested him, found him true to it — and became Muslim on the spot.

So the closing line of ayah 20 lands with full weight: "those who have lost themselves will not believe." Ibn Kathir calls it "the ultimate loss" — refusing a matter this clear, announced by the previous Prophets. Maʿārif: those who know his true identity and still refuse are simply ruining themselves at their own hands.

## The gravest wrong (ayah 21)

Ayah 21 asks who could do greater wrong (*ẓulm*) than the one guilty of two crimes, and it names them both: inventing a lie against Allah (such as claiming Allah sent him when He did not, Ibn Kathir explains), and rejecting Allah's proofs, signs and evidences when they come. Ibn Kathir's verdict covers both: neither the forger nor the denier will ever acquire success.

## The long standing before the trial (ayah 22)

Ayah 22 opens the scene the whole passage has been building toward: "the Day We gather them all together" — Maʿārif: the disbelievers *and their self-made objects of worship* — "then We shall say to those who associated partners: Where are your partners whom you used to assert?" Ibn Kathir notes the same summons in 28:62.

Maʿārif draws a striking point from a single word: *thumma* ("then, after that") denotes delay. The questioning will not begin the moment they are gathered. They will stand in wonder and perplexity for a long stretch of time before the reckoning commences. In a hadith the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said: what would happen to you when Allah gathers you on the plains of Resurrection "as arrows are gathered in the quiver" — and you remain in that state for fifty thousand years? And another narration — this one reported by Ḥākim in Al-Mustadrak and by Al-Bayhaqī — says that everyone will tarry in the dark on that Day for one thousand years, unable even to talk to one another. Both figures appear in the Qur'an itself — fifty thousand years in 70:4, a thousand years in 22:47 — and Maʿārif reconciles them: the Day's length will be *felt* according to the severity of one's suffering, so it will seem like fifty thousand years to some and a thousand to others. So long will the wait be, Maʿārif adds, that people will *wish* for the reckoning to begin, whatever the outcome, just to be relieved of the uncertainty.

## The false oath (ayah 23)

When the question finally comes, ayah 23 records the idolaters' answer — and calls it their *fitnah*. Ibn Kathir explains the word as their "argument"; ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurasānī reads it as: no plea will be left to them in the face of the affliction placed upon them. Maʿārif allows both classical senses of fitnah — "trial" and "infatuation": their answer is itself a trial; and all their lifelong infatuation with the idols, for which they even made sacrifices, is gone on the day they must disown them.

And what an answer it is: **"By Allah, our Lord, we were never mushrikīn"** — a lie, sworn by Allah's own great name, before their very Lord, on the Day of Retribution. Maʿārif calls it astonishing, and reports two explanations. Most commentators say it is not calculated at all: the sheer terror of the Day makes them utter what they do not intend. But Maʿārif also offers a deeper reading: Allah deliberately leaves them free to speak as they spoke in the world, so that all creation can see their full profile — that these people were not only disbelievers but unmatched liars, who would not desist from lying even on so horrifying an occasion. Surah Al-Mujādalah hints at exactly this: *"they will swear to Him as they swear to you"* (58:18).

Then comes the demonstration of power. Their mouths are sealed and their own limbs are commanded to speak — as Surah Yā Sīn says: *"That Day We shall set a seal on their mouths, but their hands will speak to Us and their feet bear witness to all that they did"* (36:65). Their hands, feet, eyes and ears turn out to have been, in Maʿārif's phrase, secret-service agents who were with them all along. This is how Ibn ʿAbbās reconciled this ayah with 4:42 ("they shall not conceal anything from Allah"): first they lie as much as they can, even on oath — but once their own hands and feet testify against them, no one has the courage to say anything false again. The wrongdoer is given full freedom to put his statement on record in the court of the Judge of judges; Allah then demolishes the facade of his lie through the testimony of his own body.

Maʿārif sets this beside the questioning in the grave to show why the two work differently. When the angels Munkar and Nakīr ask the disbeliever "Who is your Lord and what is your religion?", the hadith says he answers "I do not know" — no one can lie in *that* test, because the angels have no knowledge of the unseen and cannot summon the limbs as witnesses; if lying were possible there, the whole system would be disturbed. Before Allah, by contrast, lying is permitted — and utterly futile.

Two further notes from Maʿārif deserve attention. First, who exactly are these sworn deniers? Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ and Mazharī report from some elders that they are people who never openly declared a created being to be God — but in practice assigned the powers of Godhood to creatures: seeking their needs from them, making offerings in their names, asking them for sustenance, health and children. *They did not consider themselves mushriks* — so on that Day they will swear they were not, until Allah exposes their disgrace. It is a sobering thought: shirk can live in a heart that has never once called itself idolatrous. Second, the technical question of how Allah addresses them here when other verses say He will not speak to the disbelievers: the speech negated there is the speech of honour and acceptance, not of admonition — or, it is said, this address may come through the angels.

## The lie that vanishes (ayah 24)

Ayah 24 turns to the Prophet ﷺ: "See how they lie against themselves" — the curse of the lie falls back on no one but its teller — "and lost to them is what they used to invent." Maʿārif opens up several faces of that *iftirāʾ* (fabrication): it may be the shirk itself, a worldly fabrication whose reality is exposed on the Day of Resurrection; or the false oath just sworn, demolished by the limbs' testimony; or — as some commentators say — the interpretations they used to dress their idolatry in, such as the plea that they worshipped the idols only so that they would intercede with Allah and bring them closer to Him (39:3). That excuse evaporates on the Day when no intercessor appears for them and nothing reduces their punishment. Ibn Kathir cites the parallel scene in 40:73–74, where they are asked "Where is what you used to associate besides Allah?" and answer, "They have vanished from us."

Maʿārif also resolves an apparent tension: 37:22 says the wrongdoers will be gathered *with* what they used to worship, yet here the false gods are "lost." The answer: they will be physically present but absent in every way that matters — unavailable as partners, sharers or intercessors, unable to help their clients in any way; or they may be gathered together first and questioned after being separated.

## Living it

Maʿārif closes the passage with the lesson it says the false oath is there to teach: **lying is a habit that is never easy to shake off.** These people swore falsely before Muslims all their lives — and could not stop even on the Day that disgraced them before the entire creation of Allah. Hence the severity of the warnings: the Prophet ﷺ said, "Stay away from lying, because a lie is the accomplice of sins, and a lie and a sin will both go to Jahannam" (Ibn Ḥibbān in his Ṣaḥīḥ). Asked what deed could take a person to Hell, he answered: "A lie" (Musnad of Aḥmad). On the night of the Miʿrāj — the Ascent to Heaven — he was shown a man whose mouth was slit apart again and again, and when he asked Jibrāʾīl who it was, the angel answered: "He is a liar." The Musnad of Aḥmad also records: one cannot become a complete Muslim until he gives up lying altogether — even in joke or fun. And Al-Bayhaqī and others report on sound authority that a Muslim's character may carry other bad traits — but never breach of trust and lying; a further narration adds that lying decreases one's sustenance (rizq).

Alongside that stands the passage's other standing duty, from ayah 19: everyone the Qur'an reaches is, in Saʿīd ibn Jubayr's words, like one who has visited Muhammad ﷺ himself — warned by it, and charged to pass it on, even if only one ayah. Between those two — a tongue purged of lies and a tongue that carries the Book — lies the difference between the witnesses who stand firm on that Day and those whose only testimony is an oath that collapses.

passages.title: Sealed hearts and the denial of resurrection
passages.tafsir:
These eight ayat are a complete anatomy of disbelief. They begin inside the disbeliever as he sits listening to the Qur'an in this world (ayat 25–26), then leap forward to show that same person standing at the edge of the Fire and then before his Lord on the Day of Resurrection (27–30), and close with the verdict — total loss — and the diagnosis of what deceived him: mistaking this worldly life for the only reality (31–32). What binds the passage together is one claim, made from several angles: unbelief is not caused by a shortage of evidence. It is a condition of the heart — and if it is not healed in this life, it persists even into the next world, where the disbeliever's very regrets turn out to be lies.

## The heart that hears but cannot hear (ayat 25–26)

Ibn Kathir explains that these people actually came to the Prophet ﷺ and physically heard him recite the Qur'an — but the recitation did not benefit them, "because Allah has set veils on their hearts, and so they do not understand the Qur'an." The Arabic word for these veils is *akinnah*, coverings placed over the heart so that it cannot grasp (*yafqahūhu* — understand) what the ears are receiving; and in their ears is *waqr*, a deafness that blocks precisely "what benefits them." The faculty of hearing works; the faculty of taking guidance from what is heard does not. Ibn Kathir sets beside this Allah's words elsewhere: the example of those who disbelieve "is as that of him who shouts at one who hears nothing but calls and cries" (2:171) — the sound arrives, but nothing of its meaning does.

That it is Allah who set these veils is stated plainly — "We have set veils on their hearts" — and we affirm it as He said it. But Ibn Kathir's own cross-reference shows this is no arbitrary decree: he cites, "Had Allah known of any good in them, He would indeed have made them listen" (8:23). The seal answers to what is in the person.

The proof that the problem lies in the heart, not the evidence, is the next clause: "if they see every one of the ayat they will not believe therein." *Āyāt* here means signs, proofs, clear evidences — and Ibn Kathir comments that no quantity of them will move people who "do not have sound comprehension or fair judgment." So instead of believing, they come to argue, "using falsehood against truth," and produce their best explanation of the Qur'an: *asāṭīr al-awwalīn*, "tales of the men of old." Ibn Kathir spells out what this accusation meant: the Qur'an, they claimed, was taken from the books of those who came before — plagiarized. Faced with revelation, the most they could manage was to call it second-hand.

Ayah 26 then adds action to attitude: "They prevent others from him, and they themselves keep away from him." Ibn Kathir notes that this combines two evils in one sentence: "they neither benefit themselves, nor let others benefit from the Prophet ﷺ." On the widely held reading — from Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, Qatadah, Mujahid, ad-Dahhak and others — this describes the disbelievers of Quraysh generally: "they used to refrain from meeting Muhammad ﷺ and they discouraged people from coming to him." Ibn 'Abbas, in the report of 'Ali bin Abi Talhah, said it means they hinder people from believing in him.

But Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records a second, more piercing reading, also reported from Ibn 'Abbas (cited via Mazhari, with a narration by Ibn Abi al-Hatim from Sa'id ibn Abi Hilal): the ayah concerns Abu Talib and the Prophet's ﷺ other uncles, who stopped people from causing him pain — they shielded him, even supported him — yet would not themselves believe in the Qur'an or follow it. On this reading the pronoun refers to the Prophet ﷺ himself, not to the Qur'an: they forbade harm *to him*, while keeping their own hearts *away from him*. It is a sobering possibility: a person can spend his strength defending the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and still hold himself back from the one step that would save him.

Either way, the ending is the same: "they destroy none but themselves, yet they perceive it not." Ibn Kathir: the harm of this behaviour "will only touch them" — and they cannot even feel it happening.

## The wish that is a lie (ayat 27–30)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān introduces this scene by recalling that Islam rests on three basic principles — Tawhid (the Oneness of Allah), Risalah (prophethood), and Akhirah (the Hereafter) — and that of the three, belief in the Akhirah has "pragmatically the most revolutionary effects," because it channels every human deed into a particular direction. These verses press on exactly that nerve.

In ayah 27 the deniers are made to stand at the Fire — Ibn Kathir pictures them witnessing "its chains and restraints" with their own eyes — and they cry out: "Would that we were but sent back! Then we would not deny the ayat of our Lord, and we would be of the believers!"

Ayah 28 opens with the devastating word *bal* — "Nay." Allah rejects the wish on two grounds. First, "what they had been concealing before has become manifest to them." Ibn Kathir offers two meanings as possibilities: it may mean the disbelief, denial and rebellion they used to hide in their hearts is now uncovered; or it may mean the *truth* they had known all along has surfaced — for many of them always knew, inwardly, that what the Messengers brought was true, and denied out of arrogance, as Allah said of Fir'awn and his people: "they belied them... though they were themselves convinced thereof" (27:14). Second: "if they were returned, they would certainly revert to that which they were forbidden. And indeed they are liars." Ibn Kathir explains that the plea to return is not a longing for faith at all — it is fear of the torment standing before their eyes. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls it "mere absence of choice": the compulsion of circumstances dressed up as repentance. It then unpacks why Allah calls the wish itself a lie: because the promise would never in fact be kept; and because even as they speak it, there is no true intention behind it — they are saying it "simply to buy time and avoid punishment."

Ayah 29 delivers the proof. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that "and they said: there is nothing but our worldly life, and never shall we be resurrected" links back grammatically to *ʿādū* ("they would revert") in verse 28: if returned to the world, this is what they would say *again* — while standing on the far side of the very Resurrection they deny. How is that even possible? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers: denial does not require inner uncertainty. Like the disbelievers of our own age who know Islamic realities and keep to their denial out of hostility, and like what was said of the Jews — that they recognized the Last Prophet ﷺ as they would recognize their sons, yet remained bent on opposing him — these people would deny out of sheer obstinacy and hostility, with certainty intact underneath. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then relates that the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said that at the reckoning, Allah will ask Adam (peace be upon him) to stand near the Scale of Justice, look at the deeds of his progeny, and allow anyone whose good deeds outweigh his sins to go to Paradise — and Allah will say of the one admitted to the punishment of Hell: this is the one about whom I know that, if sent to the world again, he would do the same as he did before. The sentence is not passed on a moment of weakness; it is passed on what Allah knows, in His eternal knowledge, the person would always choose.

Ayah 30 completes the movement, and its scene mirrors ayah 27: there they were made to stand at the Fire; here, before their Lord Himself. One question is put to them: "Is this not the truth?" — Ibn Kathir: is the Resurrection not real, contrary to everything you claimed? And they answer with an oath: "Yes, by our Lord!" — the tongue now swearing by Allah to the very truth it spent a lifetime denying. The reply is final: "So taste the torment, because you used not to believe."

## "Indeed they are liars" — the passage's warning about lying

In ayah 28 Allah brands their words plainly: "indeed they are liars." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses over the unsettling implication. Lying is an evil habit "which is never easy to shake off" — so much so that people who used to swear falsely before Muslims during their life in this world were "unable to stop lying even on the fateful day of Resurrection," which put them to disgrace before the entire creation of Allah. It then gathers the warnings of the Sunnah. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Stay away from lying, because a lie is the accomplice of sins, and a lie and a sin will both go to Jahannam" — that is, to Hell (recorded by Ibn Hibban in his Sahih). Asked what deed could take a person to Hell, he ﷺ answered: a lie (the Musnad of Ahmad). And in another narration from the Musnad of Ahmad: one cannot become a complete Muslim until he gives up lying altogether — not even lying by way of joke or fun. Al-Baihaqi and others record, on sound authority, that a Muslim's character may bear other bad traits — but not breach of trust, and not lying. And on the night of the Mi'raj (the Ascent to Heaven), the Prophet ﷺ saw a man the corners of whose mouth were being slit apart, then restored, then slit apart again; he asked Jibra'il who it was, and was told: "He is a liar." The link to our passage is direct: a habit indulged in the world becomes a fixture of the self — and the self is what a person carries into the Hereafter.

## The verdict, and what deceived them (ayat 31–32)

"Losers indeed are those who deny the meeting with Allah (*liqāʾ Allah*) — until the Hour comes upon them all of a sudden (*baghtatan*)," and they cry "*yā ḥasratanā*" — "Alas for us, that we gave no thought to it!" Ibn Kathir describes this as the regret of the disbelievers when facing Allah, their sorrow over the good they never did and the evil they did do; and he notes that the "it" they gave no thought to may be this worldly life itself, or the affairs of the Hereafter. Then the image: "they will bear their burdens (*awzār*) on their backs — and evil indeed are the burdens they will bear."

Ibn Kathir relates, through Asbat, from As-Suddi a vivid account of these burdens: upon entering the grave, the unjust person meets a companion of ugly face, foul odor and dirty clothes. "How ugly is your face!" — "So was your work." "Who are you?" — "I am your deeds." The companion stays with him in the grave, and on the Day of Resurrection says: "In the life of the world, I used to carry you, because you followed desire and lust. Today, you carry me" — and he rides on the unjust person's back and leads him until he enters the Fire. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that hadith narrations describe the reverse for the righteous: on the day of Qiyamah the good person's deeds become his *ride*, while the evil person's deeds are placed on him like a burden. The same deeds; only who carries whom is different.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws from this whole scene the passage's deepest theological point. Through all the panic — the false swearing, the pleas to be sent back — not one of them says: *"Now we have believed, and from now on we will do nothing but good."* They cannot, because the Hereafter is not *Dār al-ʿAmal*, the Venue of Deeds; the door of action has closed. And sound iman (faith) must be *bil-ghayb* — belief in the Unseen. Confirming what stands physically before your eyes is not the attestation faith requires; it is merely acting in line with what you have personally seen. Everything — faith, its fruits, the pleasure of Allah, Paradise itself — can be earned "only (repeat, only) through the life of the present world, neither before, nor after."

Which is why ayah 32 turns, finally, to how that one life is spent. "And the life of this world is nothing but play (*laʿib*) and amusement (*lahw*)." Ibn Kathir immediately adds a precision: *most* of it is play and amusement. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān guards against the wrong conclusion: what is censured is not life itself but the time of life "spent being heedless to the thought and concern of Allah." Life itself is a great blessing and "an asset of unmatched value" — which is exactly why suicide is forbidden as haram (unlawful), and why even praying or wishing for death is prohibited: it is ingratitude for the blessing. A hadith cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says: the dunya (this world) is cursed, and cursed is what is in it, except the Dhikr (remembrance) of Allah, or a person of knowledge, or a student. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Imam al-Jazri's clarification that *everything* done in conformity with obedience to Allah counts as His remembrance — all permissible ways of earning a livelihood, and the fulfilment of the rights of family, relatives, friends, neighbours and guests, which have themselves been identified as acts of charity and worship. Nothing you own is dearer than your time in this world, and no one knows whether his remaining share is seventy years, seventy hours, or the span of a single breath.

So the passage ends on the very faculty it began with. In ayah 25 the veiled heart could not understand; ayah 32 closes by holding understanding out to whoever will take it: "But far better is the abode of the Hereafter for those who have taqwa (mindfulness of Allah). Will you not then understand?" And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān seals it with the Prophet's ﷺ reported words: wise is he who controls his self, stays pleased with minimal resources, and devotes his deeds to what is after death.

passages.title: Consoling the grieved Prophet over their rejection
passages.tafsir:
This passage is Allah's direct consolation to His Messenger ﷺ: his own people were calling his message a lie, and Allah Himself opens by telling him that He knows how much their words grieve him. The four ayat form a single movement of comfort — Allah tells him *I see your grief, and it is not truly you they reject* (ayah 33), *you are not the first, and the outcome is already decreed* (ayah 34), *even a miracle would not open a heart that Allah has not opened* (ayah 35), and finally *only the living hear; the dead must wait for the Resurrection* (ayah 36). The tafsir — verse-by-verse commentary on the Qur'an — of Ibn Kathir treats the whole section under a single heading: **Comforting the Prophet ﷺ**.

## "We certainly know what grieves you"

Ayah 33 opens with something remarkably tender: قَدْ نَعْلَمُ — *We certainly know* — that what they say grieves you. Before any argument or instruction, Allah simply acknowledges the pain. Ibn Kathir explains: "We know about their denial of you and your sadness and sorrow for them" — note the two directions of that grief: sorrow at being rejected, and sorrow *for* the rejecters themselves. Ibn Kathir connects this to a family of ayat with the same concern, where Allah says "So destroy not yourself in sorrow for them" (35:8), "It may be that you are going to kill yourself with grief, that they do not become believers" (26:3), and "Perhaps you would kill yourself in grief over their footsteps… because they believe not in this narration" (18:6). The picture that emerges across these ayat is of a Prophet ﷺ whose compassion for his people was so intense that revelation repeatedly had to address it.

## "It is not you they deny"

Then comes the heart of the consolation: *it is not you that they deny; it is the verses of Allah that the wrongdoers reject*. The Arabic draws a contrast between two words. They do not يُكَذِّبُونَكَ — call *you* a liar — rather they بِآيَاتِ اللَّهِ يَجْحَدُونَ, they *reject* the signs of Allah. Ibn Kathir puts it plainly: "they do not accuse you of being a liar… it is only the truth that they reject and refuse." Their quarrel was never with Muhammad ﷺ the man; their quarrel was with the truth he carried.

The narrations preserved in the sources prove this in the opponents' own words, and they are worth telling in full.

**The three nights.** Ibn Kathir relates, through Muhammad bin Ishaq from Az-Zuhri, that Abu Jahl, Abu Sufyan Sakhr bin Harb and Al-Akhnas bin Shurayq each came out one night to listen secretly to the Prophet ﷺ reciting the Qur'an, none aware that the others had come. They listened until morning, then met each other on the way back, and vowed never to repeat it "so that the young men of Quraysh would not hear of what they did and imitate them." The next night each came back, assuming the others would keep the vow. They were caught again, criticized one another, and vowed again. On the third night the same thing happened. These men could not stay away from the very recitation they publicly called a lie. During the day that followed, Al-Akhnas took his staff and went to Abu Sufyan in his house and asked his honest opinion; Abu Sufyan admitted, "By Allah, I have heard some things that I recognize and know their implications," though other things remained unclear to him — and Al-Akhnas confessed the same. Then Al-Akhnas went to Abu Jahl, who gave the most revealing answer of all: we competed with Banu 'Abd Manaf — the Prophet's ﷺ subtribe — feeding as they fed and giving as they gave, until we were neck and neck with them "just as two horses in a race"; and now they say a Prophet has arisen among them to whom revelation comes from the heaven — "how can we ever beat them at that? By Allah, we will never believe in him or accept what he says." Not *he is lying*, but *we cannot afford for it to be true*.

**Abu Jahl's private confession.** The second commentary this passage draws on, Maʿārif ul-Qurʾān — a tafsir of the Qur'an — adds a narration it cites from Tafsir Mazhari, an earlier commentary it quotes, on the authority of As-Suddiy: Al-Akhnas and Abu Jahl, two chiefs of the Quraysh tribe, once met completely alone, and Al-Akhnas pressed him — no third person is listening to us; tell me what you really think about Muhammad ibn 'Abdullah: is he telling the truth or not? Abu Jahl swore by Allah: "No doubt, Muhammad is true. He has never lied all his life." His objection was tribal rivalry, not doubt: the Banu Qusayy branch of Quraysh already held the flag, the duty of providing water for the Hajj pilgrims, and the keys of the Kaʿbah as its custodians — "if we are to accept that the station of prophethood also belongs to them, what will the rest of the Quraysh be left with?" (Maʿārif ul-Qurʾān notes the bitter irony in his very name: in Arabia he was called Abul-Hikam, "man of wisdom," but his hostility to Islam earned him the name history remembers — Abu Jahl, "man of ignorance.") In another narration, reported from Najiyah ibn Kaʿb, Abu Jahl said it to the Prophet ﷺ himself: "We do not suspect you of lying, nor do we belie you, but we belie the Book or Religion which you have come up with."

**Two readings of the ayah.** Based on these narrations, Maʿārif ul-Qurʾān says the ayah can be taken in its plain sense: the disbelievers did not truly consider him ﷺ a liar; their denial was aimed at the signs of Allah. But it also allows a second sense: even where they did outwardly belie him, the real outcome of that belying was itself the belying of Allah and His signs — as conveyed in a hadith cited in that commentary, that whoever causes pain to the Prophet ﷺ is liable to be judged as causing pain to Allah. On either reading the consolation is the same: *the wound is not yours to carry alone; the offence is against Allah, and Allah will answer for it.*

## The consolation of precedent — and an unalterable decree

From the Prophet's ﷺ own grief, the passage now widens the lens to the long line of Messengers before him. *Messengers before you were denied, and they bore the denial and the harm with patience, until Our help reached them.* Ibn Kathir draws three things from this: it comforts the Prophet ﷺ by placing him in the company of the mighty Messengers before him; it commands him to be patient as they were patient; and it carries a promise — victory came to those Messengers in this life just as it is theirs in the Hereafter, and the same good end awaits him.

Then the anchor of the whole passage: وَلَا مُبَدِّلَ لِكَلِمَاتِ اللَّهِ — *none can alter the Words of Allah*. Ibn Kathir explains that this refers to Allah's decision that victory in this world and the next belongs to His believing servants, and he cites the decree in Allah's own words elsewhere: "And verily Our Word has gone forth of old for Our servants, the Messengers: that they verily would be made triumphant, and that Our hosts, they verily would be the victors" (37:171–173), and "Allah has decreed: Verily, it is I and My Messengers who shall be the victorious" (58:21). The ayah closes: *surely the news of the Messengers has already reached you* — you know their stories, Ibn Kathir says, you know they were given victory and prevailed over those who rejected them, "and you have a good example in them."

## The tunnel and the ladder

Ayah 35 turns to the Prophet's ﷺ longing to do *something more* — anything — to bring his people to faith. *If their aversion is hard on you, then if you can, seek a tunnel into the earth or a ladder into the sky to bring them a sign…* Ibn 'Abbas, in the report of 'Ali bin Abi Talhah, unpacks the image: "If you were able to seek a tunnel and bring them an Ayah, or go up a ladder in the sky and bring a better Ayah than the one I (Allah) gave them, then do that" — and similar was reported from Qatadah, As-Suddi and others. It is deliberately an impossible offer. Dig into the earth, climb to the sky itself, produce a sign more dazzling than the one already given — it would change nothing, because the obstacle was never a shortage of evidence. The three-nights story has already shown us why: they had heard the sign, recognized it, and turned away out of rivalry.

Then the theological core: *had Allah willed, He could have gathered them all together upon guidance*. Ibn Kathir pairs it with the ayah, "And had your Lord willed, those on earth would have believed, all of them together." Guidance is in Allah's hand alone. Ibn 'Abbas explains the ayah's ending — *so be not one of the ignorant* — with great gentleness: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was eager that all people believe and be guided to follow him. Allah told him that only those whose happiness Allah has written in the first Dhikr will believe" — that is, those for whom felicity was written in Allah's original decree. The "ignorance" being warned against here is not any fault in the Prophet ﷺ; it is the mistaken assumption — natural to a heart that loves people — that enough effort or enough proof can force faith into being. That door belongs to Allah.

## Only the living hear

Ayah 36 answers the question ayah 35 leaves hanging — if no sign can force faith, who then will believe? *Only those who listen will respond*. Ibn Kathir: only those who "hear the speech, comprehend and understand it" will accept the call. And the others? *As for the dead, Allah will raise them up; then to Him they will be returned.* Ibn Kathir says "the dead" here are the disbelievers — because their hearts are dead. Allah likens them to dead corpses as a way of mocking and belittling them: preaching to a heart that has killed its own receptivity is like preaching at a graveside. He connects it to another ayah: the Qur'an gives warning "to him who is living, and that the Word may be justified against the disbelievers" (36:70). But the ayah does not end at their deadness — *Allah will raise them up, then to Him they will be returned*. The hearts that refused to live in this world will be made to stand in the next, and the reckoning they ignored will find them.

## What this passage teaches

For anyone who carries truth to people who will not receive it — a parent, a teacher, a caller to Allah — this passage draws the lines with precision. Grief at rejection is not a flaw; Allah acknowledged it in His Messenger ﷺ before correcting anything. Rejection of the message is rarely an honest verdict on the evidence — Abu Jahl swore in private to the truth he fought in public — so do not take it as a verdict on yourself. Your task is the task of the Messengers in ayah 34: patience under denial and harm, in certainty that Allah's decreed help comes and none can alter His Words. And the results are not yours to force: no tunnel into the earth and no ladder into the sky will open a heart Allah has not opened. Speak to the living — those who listen — and leave the dead to the One who will raise them, for to Him they will all be returned.

passages.title: Demands for signs answered by Allah's living creation
passages.tafsir:
This passage answers the idolaters' standing demand — "show us a miracle and then we will believe" — by turning their eyes to the signs already surrounding them and already inside them. Ayah 37 records the demand and explains why it is refused; ayah 38 replies that the living creation itself is a sign — every creature on earth a community like ours, recorded, provided for, and destined to be gathered; ayah 39 diagnoses why people can stand amid such signs and perceive nothing; and ayat 40–41 close the argument by summoning a witness the idolaters cannot dismiss: their own hearts in a moment of terror, which call on Allah alone. The five ayat hold together as one movement — a demand for a sign, answered by signs, ending with the sign each denier carries within himself.

## The demand for a miracle — and the wisdom in refusing it (ayah 37)

Ibn Kathir explains that the idolaters kept saying, "Why does not Muhammad bring an ayah from his Lord?" — meaning, he notes, *a miracle of their choice*. The word **ayah** is the Qur'an's word for a sign; it is used both for a verse of revelation and for a miracle. What they wanted was spectacle on demand, as in their taunt elsewhere: "We shall not believe in you, until you cause a spring to gush forth from the ground for us" (17:90).

The Qur'an's reply is not that such a sign is impossible: "Say: Allah is certainly able to send down a sign, but most of them know not." What most of them do not know, Ibn Kathir explains, is why the sign is withheld. Allah decided out of His wisdom to delay it — because if He sent a sign of their liking and they still did not believe, this would hasten their punishment, as happened with the previous nations. He cites Allah's words: "And nothing stops Us from sending the Ayat but that the people of old denied them. And We sent the she-camel to Thamud as a clear sign, but they did her wrong" (17:59). Thamud were given a clear sign and wronged her — and it is their like whose punishment was hastened. So the refusal that looked to the demanders like weakness was in fact a protection: withholding the sign spared them the fate of the nations before them. And had the aim been mere submission, that too was easy for Him: "If We will, We could send down to them from the heaven a sign, to which they would bend their necks in humility" (26:4).

## Communities like you (ayah 38)

"There is not a moving creature on earth, nor a bird that flies with its two wings, but are **umam** like you."

*Umam* is the plural of *ummah* — the word the Qur'an uses for a community or nation. The early commentators cited by Ibn Kathir unfold it: Mujahid said it means the various species with their distinct names; Qatadah said, "Birds are an Ummah, humans are an Ummah and the Jinns are an Ummah"; As-Suddi said it means creations, or species. Every kind of creature is a nation — known to Allah, provided for by Him, its affairs never forgotten. To people demanding one dazzling sign, the ayah answers: the earth is already full of them.

Then: "**We have neglected nothing in the Book.**" Ibn Kathir explains this as Allah's all-embracing knowledge: the knowledge of all things is with Allah, and He never forgets any of His creatures, their sustenance, or their affairs, whether they live in the sea or on land. He connects it to "And no moving creature is there on earth but its provision is due from Allah. And He knows its dwelling place and its deposit. All is in a Clear Book" (11:6) — a record, he says, of their names, numbers, movements, and lack of movement — and to "And so many a moving creature there is, that carries not its own provision! Allah provides for it and for you" (29:60). The creature that cannot carry its own provision is fed; the same Lord feeds you.

**"Then unto their Lord they shall be gathered."** Ibn Kathir records two readings from the early authorities. Ibn 'Abbas — as Ibn Abi Hatim reported — said, "Death gathers them." It was also said that the Day of Resurrection gathers them, citing "And when the wild beasts shall be gathered together" (81:5). On this second reading Ibn Kathir brings the report recorded by 'Abdur-Razzaq from Abu Hurayrah: all creatures will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection — the beasts, birds and all others — and Allah's justice will be so perfect that the un-horned sheep will receive retribution from the horned sheep. Then Allah will command them, "Be dust!" — and it is at that moment that the disbeliever will say, "Woe to me! Would that I were dust!" (78:40). Ibn Kathir notes that this was reported from the Prophet ﷺ in the Hadith about the Trumpet. Maarif ul Quran gives a narration of Abu Hurairah reported by Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Baihaqi in the same sense: on the Day of Qiyamah all animals, beasts and birds will be given life once again, and such will be the measure of divine justice that a horned animal which had hit the hornless one shall be subjected to retaliation; when all injustices have been vindicated, all of them will be commanded to become dust — and the disbeliever will wish that he too were dust, and thus saved from the punishment of Hell. In another narration from Abu Hurairah, Imam Al-Baghawi reports that the Prophet ﷺ said: on the Day of Qiyamah the rights of all holders of rights shall be vindicated, to the limit that a hornless goat shall be vindicated against the horned one.

Maarif ul Quran draws out a point of creed and of conduct here. Animals are not obligated to observe the precepts of any Shari'ah — only human beings and jinn carry that responsibility, and reward and punishment do not apply to the non-obligated. So why retaliation between animals? The 'ulama' answer: not because the animals are accountable, but because of the Lord's utmost regard for equity and justice — the cruelty of one living creature against another will be recompensed, and then no further reward or punishment follows for them. And the lesson cuts at us, not at the sheep: if the mutual rights of creatures are so serious that even non-obligated animals are not left outside the reckoning, what of the rights human beings trample? Maarif ul Quran adds, with regret, that there are even many religiously observant people who act negligently precisely here.
