## Deaf and dumb in the darknesses (ayah 39)

Why, then, does anyone stand amid a world of signs and see nothing? Ayah 39 answers: "Those who reject Our Ayat are deaf and dumb in darkness." Ibn Kathir explains the image: because of their ignorance, little knowledge and minute comprehension, the deniers are like a deaf-mute who cannot hear nor speak, and who is, on top of that, blinded by darkness. How, he asks, can such a person find guidance to the path or change the condition he is in? He sets beside it the parable of the fire-kindler whose light is taken away — "They are deaf, dumb, and blind, so they return not" (2:17–18) — and the layered darkness of the vast deep sea, wave upon wave topped by dark clouds, where a man who stretches out his hand can hardly see it: "And he for whom Allah has not appointed light, for him there is no light" (24:40).

Then the ayah ends: "Allah sends astray whom He wills and He guides on the straight path whom He wills." Ibn Kathir's comment is plain: "for He does what He wills with His creatures." Notice how the ayah holds two truths in one breath. It lays the deafness and dumbness at the door of the deniers themselves — it is *those who reject Our Ayat* who end up in the dark — and in the same breath it affirms that guidance and misguidance are in Allah's hand alone, decreed by His will. Both are true at once: the deniers earn their darkness, and no one enters light or darkness except by the will of the Lord of both. This is also the final answer to the demand of ayah 37: the problem was never a shortage of signs, so one more sign was never going to solve it.

## The witness inside them (ayat 40–41)

Ibn Kathir opens his commentary on these two ayat by stating that Allah does what He wills with His creatures and none can resist His decision or avert what He decrees for them; He is the One Who has no partners, Who accepts the supplication from whomever He wills. Against that backdrop, the passage moves from the signs *around* the idolaters to the sign *within* them. The Prophet ﷺ is told to put a question: "Tell me, if Allah's torment comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you, would you then call upon any one other than Allah? — if you are truthful!" That last clause, Ibn Kathir explains, means: if you are truthful in taking gods besides Him. It is a challenge to their sincerity, and it needs no answer from them because ayah 41 supplies it: "Nay! To Him alone you call, and, if He willed, He would remove that distress for which you call upon Him, and you forget at that time whatever partners you joined with Him."

Ibn Kathir spells it out: you — the disbelievers — will not call on other than Allah in that case, *because you know* that none except He is able to remove the affliction. In times of necessity, he says, you call only on Allah and forget your idols and false deities: "And when harm touches you upon the sea, those that you call upon besides Him vanish from you except Him" (17:67). The partnership they argued for in comfort does not survive a moment of genuine fear. Notice too the reservation in ayah 41 — He removes the distress *if He willed*: even the answer to their desperate cry rests on His will alone, the will that none can resist and none can avert.

So the passage's argument completes its circle. They demanded one sign from heaven; Allah pointed to a world full of them — every beast and bird a community under His knowledge, provision and justice — then explained why the deniers perceive none of it, and finally called their own instincts to testify: the truth they denied in argument — that Allah alone is to be called upon — is the very truth they practise the instant catastrophe strikes. The sign they asked for was already written in creation, in the Book that neglects nothing, and in their own hearts.

**Living it.** Two things follow for a believer. First, from ayah 38: the rights of Allah's creatures — human and animal — are weighty enough that Allah will settle a score between two sheep; treat no wrong against another creature as too small to matter. Second, from ayat 40–41: the sincerity that disbelievers only find in disaster is what the believer is meant to live in ease — calling on Him alone before the storm, not only in it.

passages.title: How earlier nations were tested then destroyed
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah al-Anʿām 42–45: Two Tests, Two Failures, One Ending

This passage lays out, in four tightly-linked ayat, Allah's established way of dealing with nations that rejected their messengers. In Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān's framing, they were tested in two ways: first with hardship, to see whether suffering would become the cause of their turning to Allah; then — when that failed — the doors of worldly comforts were opened to them, so that through those blessings they might recognise their Benefactor and remember Him. They failed both tests, and the punishment came suddenly and, in Maʿārif's words, "destroyed them to the last man." What holds ayat 42–45 together is a single narrative arc: two tests, two failures, one ending — and a closing word of praise that reframes the whole story.

## The argument these ayat complete

The passage does not begin cold. In the ayat just before it (40–41), the disbelievers of Makkah were challenged: if Allah's punishment struck you, or the Hour itself arrived, whom would you really call upon? Allah Himself answers on their behalf: *"Nay! To Him alone you call"* — in Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān's words, at a time of such mass calamity even the greatest mushrik (one who worships others alongside Allah) will forget all about his idols and call none but Allah. Ibn Kathir connects this to the ayah, *"And when harm touches you upon the sea, those that you call upon besides Him vanish from you except Him"* (17:67).

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān then identifies the objection ayat 42–45 are answering. In every age there are people who, despite their open disobedience to Allah and His Prophet ﷺ, keep prospering — in wealth, property, influence, recognition and power. The complacent set what their own eyes witness against the messenger's warning, and — helped along by their excuse-seeking disposition and by Shayṭān — they are hoodwinked into believing that the word of the prophet is a deception or delusion. For an answer, Maʿārif says, we turn to the present verses, where Allah points out the law which applied to what happened to past communities.

## The first test: hardship meant as mercy (ayat 42–43)

Ayah 42, in Ibn Kathir's rendering: *"Verily, We sent (Messengers) to many nations before you. And We seized them with extreme poverty and loss of health so that they might believe with humility."* Ibn Kathir unpacks the two Arabic words of the ayah: **al-baʾsāʾ**, rendered "extreme poverty," is loss of wealth and diminished provisions, while **al-ḍarrāʾ**, "loss of health," covers various illnesses, diseases and pain. Between them the pair covers the two great arenas of worldly suffering — what a person has and what a person is.

The purpose is stated in the ayah itself: *laʿallahum yataḍarraʿūn* — in Maʿārif's rendering, "so that they may supplicate in humility." **Taḍarruʿ** is humble, pleading supplication: in Ibn Kathir's words, that they would "call Allah and supplicate to Him with humbleness and humility." Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān draws a striking conclusion from this phrase: the hardship sent upon a people in this world, though it outwardly looks like punishment, is in reality not punishment at all. It serves the purpose of a wake-up call designed to shake people out of their heedlessness — and as such, it is nothing but mercy. Since everyone turns to Allah naturally when in distress, the purpose was to make people turn to Him through a little hardship. Maʿārif cites the parallel ayah: *"We will make them taste a lesser punishment, leaving the greatest punishment aside, so that they may return"* (32:21).

Ayah 43 is the grieved rebuke, in Ibn Kathir's rendering: *"When Our torment reached them, why then did they not believe with humility?"* — meaning, as he explains, why do they not believe and humble themselves before Us when We test them with disaster? And the diagnosis follows in two clauses. First, *"But their hearts became hardened"* — Ibn Kathir explains: their hearts are not soft or humble. Second, *"and Shaytan made fair-seeming to them that which they used to do"* — which Ibn Kathir identifies as their shirk (associating partners with Allah), defiance and rebellion. The hardship that was meant to soften them found hearts that were not soft, and Shayṭān stood by making the old sins look beautiful still.

## The second test: the gates flung open (ayah 44)

Then comes the turn in the story that this passage is most famous for. In Ibn Kathir's rendering: *"So, when they forgot (the warning) with which they had been reminded"* — by ignoring and turning away from it — *"We opened to them the gates of every (pleasant) thing."* When hardship failed to humble them, Allah did not immediately destroy them — He gave them everything. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān frames the whole sequence as two tests: first hardships and sufferings, to see if these would become the cause of their turning to Allah; then, when they failed that and became all the more engrossed in disobedience, the doors of worldly comforts were opened so that through these blessings they could recognise their Benefactor and remember Him. They failed both. Rather than gratitude, they were "so lost in the labyrinth of luxury that they forgot all about the messages and teachings of Allah and His Messenger" — and having failed in both tests, their case before Allah became conclusively established against them.

Ibn Kathir's comment on the opened gates is chilling: "We opened the gates of provisions for them from wherever they wished, *so that We deceive them*." He immediately adds: "We seek refuge with Allah from such an end." Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān warns from this ayah that no one should be deceived by seeing the affluence of persons or groups and hasten to the conclusion that these are people on the correct path and that their life is a model of success — among them there could be some who have been picked out to be seized with sudden and grave punishment. It then cites the Prophet's ﷺ words: when you see blessings and wealth raining upon someone though he is deep in sin and disobedience, know that he is being lured into destruction — **istidrāj** — his affluence itself an indicator of his being seized in punishment (narrated by Ahmad from 'Aqabah ibn 'Amir, as in Tafsir Ibn Kathir).

Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī put the two-sided lesson memorably, in a statement Ibn Abi Hatim recorded: "Whomever Allah gives provision and he thinks that Allah is not testing him, has no wisdom. Whomever has little provision and thinks that Allah will not look at (provide for) him, has no wisdom." He then recited this very ayah and added: "By the Lord of the Ka'bah! Allah deceived these people, when He gave them what they wished, and then they were punished." Ease is a test exactly as hardship is a test; the one without wisdom misreads both.

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān also relates, through the commentator Ibn Jarir from ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit, that the Prophet ﷺ taught: when Allah wills for a nation to survive and grow, He creates in them two qualities — moderation in everything they do, and modesty and chastity, abstinence from indulging in what is not right. And when He wills to destroy a nation, He opens for them the doors of khiyānah (breach of faith): they appear to be successful in the world despite their breaches of faith and wrongdoings. Apparent worldly success under open wrongdoing, then, is no proof of being on the correct path.

The ayah's timing is deliberate: *"until in the midst of their enjoyment in that which they were given"* — Ibn Kathir mentions wealth, children and provisions — *"all of a sudden, We took them to punishment, and lo! They were plunged into destruction with deep regrets and sorrows."* The Arabic calls them *mublisūn* — as Ibn Kathir puts it, they have no hope for any type of good thing. The blow lands in the very midst of the enjoyment.

## The uprooting — and the praise (ayah 45)

Ibn Kathir renders the final ayah: *"So the roots of the people who did wrong were cut off. And all the praises and thanks be to Allah, the Lord of the all that exists."* Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān says the wrongdoing people were uprooted to the last man, and recalls what forms this took: the people of Nūḥ (peace be upon him) deluged in the great flood which did not spare even mountain peaks; the people of ʿĀd hit by an eight-day wind storm which left not one survivor; the people of Thamūd destroyed through a terrifying sound; the entire habitation of the people of Lūṭ (peace be upon him) overturned — its remnants, Maʿārif notes, still existing in the west of Jordan as a low-lying water in which no sea life survives, called the Dead Sea and also the Sea of Lūṭ. And, it adds, it has also happened that such peoples simply died away naturally, leaving no one behind to remember them.

Then the ayah ends in a way that might surprise a first-time reader: praise — immediately after destruction? Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān explains the hint in the words "And praise be to Allah, the Lord of the worlds": whenever the wrongdoers and the unjust are visited by some punishment or calamity, that is a blessing for the whole world, for which people should be grateful.

## Reading providence rightly

Beneath the narrative, this passage corrects how we read the world — and Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān draws the theology out explicitly. This world is **Dār al-ʿAmal**, the place where one must do what one should, not **Dār al-Jazāʾ**, the place of recompense; the real reward and punishment will come on the Day of Qiyāmah, known as the Day of Judgement or the Day of Retribution. So worldly comfort and worldly pain are not verdicts. Some hardships are sent in this world as a *sample* of punishment and some comforts as a *sample* of reward — a token of mercy from Allah. Maʿārif even relays a saying of some spiritual masters, whom it does not name, that all the comforts of the world are indicators of the comforts of Paradise, so that one learns to long for them, and all its hardships and sorrows indicators of the punishment of the Hereafter, so that one prepares to stay safe against them — for unless a sample is in sight, no one can be persuaded towards anything or warned away from any danger. Maʿārif offers a vivid analogy: this whole world is a showroom of the Ākhirah (the Hereafter), where the trader displays demonstration pieces of his merchandise in front of his shop to attract the buyer. Worldly prosperity or poverty, happiness or sorrow, are not reward and punishment in the real sense; they are a method of bringing a creation alienated from its Creator back to His fold. And, Maʿārif adds, Allah does not send down His punishment upon any people all of a sudden: punishments first come at the level of admonitions, whose purpose is to make it possible for people to shed their heedlessness and take to the correct path.

For the believer, the passage asks for two concrete postures. When hardship comes: taḍarruʿ — soften, turn, plead — because that turning is the very thing the hardship was sent to produce, and the failure of the destroyed nations was that their hearts became hardened when Allah's blows were still merciful wake-up calls. And when ease comes: self-examination rather than self-congratulation — asking, with al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī's words in mind, whether this open gate is a test being run. The one state this passage leaves no room for is the complacency of those who see open disobedience prospering and conclude that the warner must be wrong.

passages.title: Thought experiments on losing Allah's gifts
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah al-Anʿām 46–49 — Thought Experiments on Losing Allah's Gifts

This passage is a pair of piercing questions the Prophet ﷺ is commanded to put to the deniers — *imagine* your hearing, your sight, your very heart taken away; *imagine* the punishment of Allah arriving without warning — followed by the answer to both: the Messengers were sent precisely so that no one would have to face either scenario unprepared. What holds the four ayat together is a single movement from argument to invitation: two thought experiments put to the deniers (46–47), then the two real outcomes that follow from how a person responds to the Messengers (48–49).

## \"Say to them…\" — who is being addressed

Ibn Kathir opens by telling us the register of this passage: Allah said to His Messenger, *say, O Muhammad ﷺ, to those rebellious liars*. These are not gentle musings; they are challenges issued to people who had heard the message and rejected it. Both ayat begin with the command **qul** — \"Say\" — and each then poses its challenge in its own form: ayah 46 with *a-raʾaytum*, ayah 47 with *a-raʾaytakum*, both rendered in the translation as \"Imagine if…\" and glossed by Ibn Kathir as \"Tell me…\". The Qur'an is asking the deniers to run a thought experiment on themselves, because the conclusion is one they cannot escape once they honestly consider it.

## The first question: the senses you did not give yourself (ayah 46)

\"Tell me, if Allah took away your hearing and your sight, and sealed up your hearts — is there a god other than Allah who could restore them to you?\"

Ibn Kathir draws out the unstated premise: Allah could take these senses **just as He gave them to you**. The question only bites because hearing and sight were never yours by right; they were endowed. He connects this to Allah's words elsewhere: \"It is He Who has created you, and endowed you with hearing, seeing\" (67:23), and \"Or who owns hearing and sight?\" (10:31). The senses are on loan from their true Owner.

Then the ayah goes deeper than the ears and eyes — to the **sealing of the heart**. Ibn Kathir offers a second layer of meaning here: the ayah may also mean that Allah would not allow the disbelievers to **benefit from these senses in religious terms**. A man can have perfect hearing and never truly hear revelation; perfect sight and never see a sign. That is why the sealing of the heart is mentioned alongside the physical senses — and why Ibn Kathir cites the ayah, \"And know that Allah comes in between a person and his heart\" (8:24). Loss of the outward faculty and loss of the inward receptivity are both in Allah's hand alone.

The rhetorical force lands in the question's second half: *is there a god other than Allah who could restore them to you?* Ibn Kathir's answer is blunt — no one except Allah is able to give these senses back if He took them. This, he says, is the whole point of the demonstration: it testifies to **Allah's Oneness in lordship** (that He alone creates, owns, and controls) and exposes everything worshipped besides Him as \"false and unworthy.\" An idol that cannot return your hearing has no claim on your worship.

**\"See how variously We explain the Ayat, yet they turn aside.\"** Ibn Kathir explains: Allah presents the Ayat in varied ways, plain and clear — and still, after all this explanation, \"they turn away from the truth **and hinder people from following it**.\" That second clause matters: in Ibn Kathir's reading, their turning aside is not a private failing only; it also blocks the path for others. Their problem was never a shortage of evidence.

## The second question: punishment by night or by day (ayah 47)

\"Tell me, if the punishment of Allah comes to you suddenly, or openly — will any be destroyed except the wrongdoing people?\"

Ibn Kathir unpacks the two words. **Baghtatan** (\"suddenly\") means while you are unaware — or during the night — striking all at once. **Jahratan** (\"openly\") means during the day, or publicly. Between them, the two words span every hour and every circumstance: night or day, caught off guard or watching it arrive in the open.

But the question ends on a note of precision, not indiscriminate terror: *will any be destroyed except the wrongdoing people?* Ibn Kathir explains who the \"wrongdoers\" are: this torment strikes only \"those who commit injustice against themselves **by associating others with Allah**\" — that is, the injustice (*ẓulm*) in view here is *shirk*, setting up partners with Allah — \"while those who worship Allah alone without partners will be saved from it, and they will have no fear or sorrow.\" He anchors this reading in another ayah of this same sūrah: \"It is those who believe and confuse not their belief with Zulm (wrong or Shirk)\" (6:82).

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān adds the thread that ties this passage to what came just before. Ayah 45 described the wrongdoers being uprooted to the last man by Allah's mass punishment — and immediately followed it with *\"And praise be to Allah, the Lord of the worlds.\"* The hint, Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān explains, is that when the unjust are visited by punishment or calamity, **that is itself a blessing for the whole world, for which people should be grateful**. The destruction of oppressors is not a tragedy for creation; it is a mercy to everyone they oppressed.

## The answer to both questions: why Messengers are sent (ayah 48)

Having posed two scenarios that leave the deniers nowhere to stand, the passage pivots: \"And We send not the Messengers except as bearers of glad tidings and as warners.\"

Ibn Kathir spells out the double role. The Messengers **bring good news** to Allah's servants and command all that is good and righteous; and they **warn** those who disbelieve of Allah's anger and of every kind of torment. In other words, the two thought experiments of ayat 46–47 are not meant to leave anyone paralysed — the warning has already been delivered, and the way out has already been shown.

Then comes the condition and the promise: \"So whoever believes and does righteous good deeds — upon them shall be no fear, nor shall they grieve.\" Ibn Kathir defines both halves. To believe and do righteous good deeds is to believe **in the heart** in what the Messengers were sent with, and to make one's works righteous **by imitating them** — inward conviction joined to outward following.

And the promise is dissected with a beautiful precision. **\"No fear upon them\"** — concerning the **future**. **\"Nor shall they grieve\"** — about the **past**, about what they missed and left behind in this world. Ibn Kathir adds the reassurance that dissolves even that backward-looking regret: \"Certainly, Allah will be the **Wali** and Protector over what they left behind.\" The believer's yesterday and tomorrow are both in trustworthy hands. Notice how this answers ayah 47 exactly: the punishment destroys only the wrongdoers, and the believers \"will have no fear or sorrow.\"

## The other outcome (ayah 49)

\"But those who deny Our Ayat — the torment will strike them for their rebelling.\"

Ibn Kathir shows that this rebelling is not a single act but a whole posture, listing four strands: **disbelieving in the Message of the Messengers, defying Allah's commands, committing what He prohibited, and transgressing His set limits.** And the torment is explicitly tied to its cause — it strikes them *for their rebelling* — so no one is struck arbitrarily. Ayah 48 and ayah 49 stand side by side as the only two endings the passage allows: belief with righteous deeds, or denial with rebellion; security from fear and grief, or the touch of the torment.

## Living it

The passage addresses deniers, but its method is for everyone. It asks you to hold your hearing, your sight, and the softness of your own heart in open palms and recognise them as gifts that only their Giver can sustain or restore — which is Ibn Kathir's whole argument for worshipping Him alone. It reminds you, through the link Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān draws to ayah 45, that even Allah's judgements upon oppressors are occasions for the world's gratitude. And it locates real security not in the senses staying intact or the calamity never coming, but in the one shelter ayah 48 names: believing in what the Messengers brought, and setting one's deeds right by their example — after which there is nothing ahead to fear and nothing behind to grieve.

passages.title: Do not dismiss the poor sincere believers
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat answer two demands the chiefs of Makkah laid before the Prophet ﷺ. The first: prove your prophethood by producing wonders of our choosing — wealth, knowledge of the future, the nature of an angel. The second, uglier one: clear your gatherings of the poor ex-slaves who surround you, so that noblemen need not sit beside them. Allah answers both with one principle that binds the passage together: worth is not measured by wealth or rank but by what Allah alone sees — hearts, sincerity, and gratitude. Ayah 50 strips prophethood of everything the Quraysh imagined it had to be; ayah 51 redirects the Prophet's ﷺ energy to those who will actually listen; ayat 52–53 forbid dismissing the poor believers and expose the elite's contempt as a divine test they failed; ayah 54 turns to those very believers with a greeting of peace and Allah's written promise of mercy; and ayah 55 closes the movement — by signs this clear, "the way of the wicked" stands out unmistakably.

## The bargain Makkah offered

The story that unlocks ayat 52–54 is preserved in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, reporting from Ibn Kathir, who takes it from Imam Ibn Jarir. Chiefs of Quraysh — ʿUtbah, Shaybah, Ibn Rabiʿah, Mutʿim ibn ʿAdiyy, Harith ibn Nawfal and others — came to the Prophet's ﷺ uncle Abu Talib and said: one thing stopping us from listening to your nephew is that the people always around him are either slaves we freed or people who lived at our mercy. We cannot attend his sittings with such lowly people present. Tell him to send them away when we come, and we will listen and think it over.

When Abu Talib relayed this, ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) suggested trying it: what harm for a few days? These believers love us and stand on no formality — they would move aside when the chiefs arrived. Then ayah 52 came down, emphatically prohibiting any such thing, and ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) came apologizing, admitting his advice had been wrong.

And who were these "lowly" people? Bilal al-Habashi, Suhayb ar-Rumi, ʿAmmar ibn Yasir, Salim the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfah, ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud, Miqdad ibn ʿAmr and other noble Companions — may Allah be pleased with them all — people, as Maʿārif puts it, the testimonial of whose nobility and honour came from the heavens.

The sources stress that this is an ancient pattern. The people of Nuh (peace be upon him) said the very same thing: "Shall we believe in you, when the meekest (of the people) follow you?" (26:111), and Nuh answered that their account was only with his Lord. Ibn Kathir notes that at first, most who followed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ were the weak — men, women, and slaves, with only a few chiefs among them. When Heraclius, emperor of Rome, questioned Abu Sufyan about the Prophet ﷺ, he asked: do the noblemen follow him or the weak? Abu Sufyan replied, "Rather the weak among them," and Heraclius said, "Such is the case with followers of the Messengers." Maʿārif adds that for scholars of earlier religions this had become an actual proof of a prophet's truthfulness — his first followers are the poor of his community.

## What a messenger is — and is not (ayat 50–51)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the three demands behind ayah 50: if you are really Allah's Messenger, bring us the treasures of the whole world; tell us everything good and bad coming to us so we can prepare; and explain how a man like us — born of parents, eating, walking in streets and bazaars — can be a messenger at all. Had you been an angel, we would have accepted you.

Ayah 50 answers with three negations and one affirmation: "I don't tell you that with me are the treasures of Allah, nor (that) I know the Unseen; nor do I tell you that I am an angel. I but follow what is revealed to me." The office of a messenger, Maʿārif explains, is not ownership of Allah's treasures, not encompassing knowledge, not angelic nature — it is simply to follow the revelation, live it, and call others to it. That is the only claim he made, and of proofs for it there was no shortage.

These, Maʿārif says, are precise rules of guidance: they clarify what a messenger of Allah really is and erase the false notions the disbelievers held about that office. And there is an instruction folded in for Muslims themselves — do not take your Messenger to be God as the Christians did, nor assign to him any proprietary right in Godhood. True realization of the prophets' greatness, and true love for them, means avoiding both excess and deficiency: the Jews did not hesitate even to kill their prophets, while the Christians turned their messenger into a God.

**Whose are the treasures?** On the word "treasures," Maʿārif notes that commentators have named many particular things, but the Qur'an itself, wherever it mentions Allah's treasures, says: "there is not a thing the treasures of which are not with Us" (15:21) — so the term embraces everything, and the named items are only examples. Then comes the pointed corollary: if the treasures of Allah are not even in the hand of the foremost of prophets and messengers, Muhammad al-Mustafa ﷺ, then to imagine that some Buzurg (pious elder) or wali (a "man of Allah") can grant whatever he wishes to whomever he chooses is, in Maʿārif's words, sheer ignorance.

**A subtle shift in wording.** The commentator Abu al-Hayyan (cited in Maʿārif from his al-Bahr al-Muhit) noticed that the first and third clauses say "I do not *say*…", while the middle clause drops that frame: not "I do not say I know the Unseen" but flatly "nor do I know the Unseen." Why? Whether he possessed the world's treasures or was an angel was a matter of plain observation — the audience could see he claimed neither, so denying the claim sufficed. But the Unseen was different: the Makkans already believed their astrologers and soothsayers knew the Unseen, and they had heard the Prophet ﷺ foretell things that then happened. So there the act itself had to be negated, not merely the claim.

**The creedal balance.** From this Maʿārif draws careful lines. The whole Umma believes that Allah blessed the Prophet ﷺ, through revelation, with knowledge of a vast number of unseen matters — surpassing the combined knowledge of angels and human beings. Yet the All-Encompassing Knowledge (al-ʿIlm al-Muhit) of the whole universe is Allah's exclusive attribute; no angel or prophet, whatever he has been given, is called ʿAlim al-Ghayb — "Knower of the Unseen" — in the Qur'an's terminology, just as none can equal Allah in being the Creator and the Provider. Claiming such equality, Maʿārif adds, is the very path of excess taken in Christianity.

The ayah ends: "Are the blind and the one who sees equal? Will you not then consider?" Ibn Kathir: is the one who is guided, following the truth, equal to the one misled? The Makkans needed only to drop obstinacy and look — their missing sight was recoverable with a little honest thought.

**Ayah 51** then tells the Prophet ﷺ where to spend himself. Maʿārif: after statements this clear, draw a line under the debating and turn to the real work of prophethood — warning "therewith," that is, with this Qur'an (Ibn Kathir), those who fear being gathered before their Lord. People stand in three classes regarding the Last Day: those certain of it, those who waver, and those who deny it outright. The call goes to all three, but the warning bears fruit soonest in the first two, so they receive special attention. And the warning itself: on that Day there will be neither protector nor intercessor besides Him — Ibn Kathir explains that no relative or intercessor can prevent His torment if He decides to punish — "so that they may have Taqwa": that awareness of standing before Allah which moves a person to good deeds now, deeds that may save him on the Day of Resurrection.

## "Do not dismiss those who call on their Lord" (ayah 52)

Notice how Allah describes the poor believers — not by lineage or wealth, the categories the chiefs cared about, but by two qualities. First: they invoke their Lord morning and evening. Ibn Kathir records from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib, Mujahid, al-Hasan and Qatadah that this refers to the obligatory prayers; Maʿārif adds that in usage "morning and evening" means all times of day and night. Second: "seeking His Face" — they want Allah Himself, with ikhlas, pure sincerity, in every act of worship. Maʿārif draws the lesson: worship without ikhlas is not trustworthy. And Ibn Kathir turns the prohibition into its positive: do not merely refrain from turning such people away — make them your companions and associates, as the parallel ayah commands: "And keep yourself patiently with those who call on their Lord morning and evening, seeking His Face" (18:28).

The middle clause — "You are accountable for them in nothing, and they are accountable for you in nothing" — carries two readings in the sources. Ibn Kathir reads it through Nuh's answer to his people: the believers' reckoning belongs to Allah alone, not to His Messenger, just as his reckoning is not up to them. Maʿārif cites Ibn ʿAtiyyah and al-Zamakhshari for a second view: the pronouns refer to the disbelieving chiefs. The Prophet ﷺ was not answerable for whether they ever believed; only if he had been could clearing the gathering for their sake even have been contemplated. Since he was not, removing the poor Muslims would be — in Maʿārif's phrase — rank injustice. Hence the verse's severe ending, addressed to the Prophet ﷺ but really shredding the chiefs' proposal: "that you may turn them away, and thus become of the wrongdoers."

## The test of some through others (ayah 53)

"Thus We have tried some of them with others." The rich were tested through the poor: would they accept a truth whose first bearers ranked beneath them? Their sneer gives the answer: "Are these the ones whom Allah favored above us?" Ibn Kathir shows this is the standing voice of privilege in the Qur'an — "Had it been a good thing, they would not have preceded us to it!" (46:11); "Which of the two groups is best in position and station?" (19:73). Maʿārif, citing the Kashshaf and other classical commentaries, makes the sharp point that this very sneer *was* the outcome of the trial: they failed it. Instead of concluding from Allah's raising of the "lowly" that nobility rests on deeds and morals, not wealth and power, they blamed Allah's choice.

The reply is a single question: "Does not Allah know best those who are grateful?" Ibn Kathir: those who thank Him in statement, action and heart — and He directs them to the ways of peace, transfers them from darkness to light, and guides them to the straight path. Ibn Kathir cites here an authentic hadith: "Allah does not look at your shapes or colors, but He looks at your heart and actions."

Maʿārif sets this in its widest frame: whenever people lose sight of the Hereafter, money quietly becomes the criterion of human worth, and the poor are stamped as low — in every age, he adds, "including ours with the loudest claims to democracy and justice." The first and last lesson of the prophets is that there is an eternal life after this one, and the standard of honour there is good morals and righteous deeds — which is why the real reckoning of who is "noble" belongs to Allah alone.

## "Peace be upon you" — mercy written (ayah 54)

Now Allah turns to the believers the chiefs wanted expelled, and honours them. "When those who believe in Our Ayat come to you, say: Salamun ʿAlaykum (peace be on you)." Maʿārif gives two meanings, both tender. Either the Prophet ﷺ is conveying to them Allah's own greeting of salam — the highest honour a human being could receive, and the perfect balm for hearts bruised by the chiefs' demand — or he is announcing their safety: whatever shortcomings they have, they stand forgiven and protected.

Maʿārif records that most commentators tie this ayah to the same event: it came to comfort ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) and those who had agreed with his advice, assuring them there would be no retribution for the past mistake — indeed blessings besides. Others read it as an independent, standing rule for every sinner who repents. There is no contradiction: by an agreed principle, a verse revealed about a specific occasion but worded generally becomes a general injunction for all.

"Your Lord has written mercy for Himself." Ibn Kathir: He has obliged His Most Honored Self to grant mercy, as a favour, out of His compassion. Maʿārif lingers on the word *Rabb* — your Nurturer and Sustainer: no nurturer lets what he nurtures go to waste; and this promise is not merely spoken but preserved in writing. The Prophet ﷺ said — in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) recorded by Imam Ahmad and found in the Two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim): "When Allah finished with the creation, He wrote in a Book that He has with Him above the Throne, 'My mercy prevails over My anger.'" Maʿārif adds the report of Salman (may Allah be pleased with him), who said they had seen it written in the Torah that Allah divided His mercy into a hundred parts, distributed one part over all creation — every tenderness between parents and children, brothers and sisters, husbands and wives, relatives, neighbours and friends flows from that single part — and kept the other ninety-nine with Himself.

Then the rule itself: "if any of you does evil in ignorance, and thereafter repents and does righteous good deeds, then surely, He is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful." Does "in ignorance" (bi-jahālah) restrict forgiveness to sins committed unknowingly? No — and the Arabic shows why. Maʿārif explains that the Qur'an uses *jahālah*, not *jahl*. Jahl is the opposite of knowledge; jahālah is the opposite of forbearance and dignity — ignorance displayed in conduct. Every sin, whenever committed, is an act of this practical ignorance, which is why Ibn Kathir says simply that every person who disobeys Allah does it in ignorance, and why some pious elders have said that a person who acts against any command given by Allah and His Messenger is a jāhil. So every sin — heedless or deliberate — can be forgiven through tawbah, repentance.

That repentance has two conditions in the ayah. First, tawbah itself: remorse — as the hadith puts it, repentance is another name for remorse. Second, islah, correction: a firm resolve never to return to the sin, and putting right what it damaged. Maʿārif spells this out concretely: missed prayers and fasts made up, unpaid zakah paid — the rights of Allah; wrongly taken property returned and the pardon of those you hurt sought — the rights of His servants; and if the wronged person has died or cannot be found, pray persistently for his forgiveness. And the ayah promises more than a clean slate: He is not only Ghafur, Forgiving, but Rahim, Merciful — the penitent is not merely pardoned but blessed with rewards.

## So the way of the criminals stands clear (ayah 55)

"And thus do We explain the Ayat in detail, that the way of the criminals may become manifest." Ibn Kathir: Allah details His signs — whatever people need explained in the affairs of life and religion — so that the path of the criminals who defy the Prophets is apparent and clear. He records a second reading too: so that *you*, O Muhammad ﷺ, may be aware of the way of the criminals. Either way the ayah seals the passage: once truth is laid out this plainly — what a messenger is, whom Allah honours, how His mercy is written — the two roads can no longer be confused. The seeing and the blind of ayah 50 have been shown exactly where they part.

## Living it

Maʿārif closes with instructions that flow straight from these ayat. Never look down on anyone for tattered clothes or a broken-down state — the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said that many a dust-stained, broken-down person is so dear to Allah that if he swears by Allah that a thing will be so, Allah honours his oath. Taking material affluence as the measure of human worth is an insult to humanity; the real criterion is morals and deeds. A caller to Allah must never sideline the sincere believers he already has in order to court the influential — their right comes first. And since Allah's rewards and blessings increase in the measure of gratitude, whoever wants more of His blessings should make thankfulness, in word and deed, a constant of his character.

passages.title: The Prophet's clear proof against their demands
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are a single, tightly-built reply. The disbelievers of Makkah had been demanding that the Divine punishment the Prophet ﷺ warned of should come to them posthaste — hurried forward, on the spot. Ayat 56–58 answer that demand with three declarations, each opening with the same command — *qul*, "Say" — and together they draw a precise line between what the Prophet ﷺ carries and what belongs to Allah alone. He carries clear proof; he does not carry the torment. Ibn Kathir captures the whole passage in his section heading: *the Prophet ﷺ understands what he conveys; torment is in Allah's hands, not the Prophet's.*

## Three "Say" commands, one line drawn

**Ayah 56** lays the foundation. "Say: I have been forbidden to worship those whom you invoke besides Allah." Before answering their demand for punishment, the Prophet ﷺ first closes the door on any compromise in worship — and then names what really drives their objections: "I will not follow your vain desires. If I did, I would go astray, and I would not be one of the rightly guided." What they call on him to follow are not proofs but desires, and to follow them would not be diplomacy but straying.

**Ayah 57** then states what he *does* stand on: "I am on clear proof (*bayyinah*) from my Lord, but you deny it." Ibn Kathir explains the *bayyinah* here as "a clear understanding of the Law of Allah that He has revealed to me" — the Prophet ﷺ is not guessing or relaying something he half-grasps; he stands upon revelation he clearly understands. Then comes the pivot of the whole passage: "I do not have what you are hastily seeking" — and Ibn Kathir confirms that what they were hastily seeking was **the torment**. They wanted the threatened punishment rushed forward.

The answer: "The decision (*ḥukm*) is only for Allah." Ibn Kathir unpacks this with a striking balance: "If He wills, He will punish you soon in response to your wish! If He wills, He will give you respite, out of His great wisdom." Either way the matter rests with Allah — and if the punishment is delayed, the delay itself is respite granted out of His great wisdom. Hence the ayah closes: "He declares the truth, and He is the best of judges" — *khayr al-fāṣilīn*, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders "the best decision-maker," and which Ibn Kathir glosses as "the best in reckoning between His servants."

**Ayah 58** completes the thought with a hypothetical: "If I had that which you are asking for impatiently, the matter would have been settled at once between you and I." Ibn Kathir's paraphrase is blunt: "if I have what you ask for, I will surely send down what you deserve of it." And the ayah ends, "but Allah knows best the wrongdoers" — the punishment is not shelved; it is with the One who knows exactly who deserves it.

## A famous question: does ayah 58 contradict the Angel of the Mountains?

Ibn Kathir raises a problem the attentive reader will feel. Ayah 58 says that had the punishment been in the Prophet's ﷺ hand, he would have sent it down. Yet the hadith in the Two Sahihs — from ʿAʼishah, may Allah be pleased with her — seems to show the opposite. She asked, "O Allah's Messenger ﷺ! Have you encountered a day harder than the day (of the battle) of Uhud?" He replied — in the wording of Muslim — recounting how Jibril (the angel Gabriel) appeared to him with an extraordinary offer:

> "Your people have troubled me a lot and the worst trouble was on the day of 'Aqabah when I presented myself to Ibn 'Abd Yalil bin 'Abd Kulal, who did not respond to my call. So I departed, overwhelmed with severe sorrow, proceeded on and could not relax until I found myself at Qarn Ath-Tha'alib where I raised my head towards the sky to see a cloud unexpectedly shading me. I looked up and saw Jibril in it and he called me saying, 'Indeed Allah has heard what you said to the people and what they have responded to you. Therefore, Allah has sent the Angel of the Mountains to you so that you may order him to do whatever you wish to these people.' The Angel of the Mountains called and greeted me, and then said, 'O Muhammad! verily, Allah has heard how your people responded to you and He has sent me to you so that you could order me to do what you wish. If you like, I will let Al-Akhshabayn (two mountains to the north and south of Makkah) fall on them.' The Prophet ﷺ said, No, but I hope that Allah will let them generate offspring who will worship Allah Alone, and will worship none besides Him."

Here the destruction of the disbelievers of Quraysh was placed within his reach — and he chose patience, asking Allah for respite for them, so that Allah might let them generate offspring who would not associate anything with Him in worship. So how can ayah 58 say he would have sent the punishment down?

Ibn Kathir's resolution — and Allah knows best, as he himself says — turns on who was asking. In the ayah, the disbelievers themselves demanded the torment, and the ayah states that had it been in the Prophet's ﷺ hand *at the time*, he would have sent it on them as they asked. In the hadith, the disbelievers asked for nothing; it was the angel responsible for the mountains who offered him the choice of letting the two mountains close in on them and crush them. The Prophet ﷺ "did not wish that and asked for respite out of compassion for them." The ayah answers those who demanded the punishment; the hadith shows the compassion of the one they demanded it from when no such demand was being made.

## Where the passage leads

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out the thread running onward from here. The answer to the disbelievers who were demanding that the Divine punishment come to them posthaste was given in "He is the best decision-maker" (57), and the perfect power of Almighty Allah was mentioned in "Allah knows the unjust best" (58). From here, the sūrah moves next into a description of the encompassment of the Knowledge and Power of Allah Taʿala over all conceivable data and destiny.

## Living it

Two things stand out for the believer. First, the passage models what it is to stand on *bayyinah*: the Prophet ﷺ neither bent his worship to pressure nor claimed powers he was not given. Certainty about the truth and honesty about one's limits go together — "I am on clear proof" and "I do not have what you are hastily seeking" come in the same breath. Second, the Angel of the Mountains hadith shows what filled the space where vengeance could have stood: hope. Offered the destruction of the people who had just rejected his call and left him overwhelmed with sorrow, the Prophet ﷺ looked past them to their offspring — hoping Allah would bring from them worshippers of Allah alone — and chose patience out of compassion for them. The decision belongs to Allah — and His Messenger ﷺ, given a choice, chose mercy.

passages.title: Keys of the unseen and souls in Allah's hand
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are the Qur'an's own portrait of two attributes that belong to Allah alone: knowledge from which nothing escapes, and power from which nothing is exempt. They move in one unbroken line — from the keys of the unseen (ayah 59), to your soul taken and returned every single night (ayah 60), to the angels who guard you in life and collect you at death (ayah 61), to the final standing before the True Master for judgment (ayah 62). What binds them into a unit is a single sweeping claim: from the fall of a leaf to the departure of your soul, everything is in Allah's hand.

## Why the passage opens with "and with Him…"

Ibn Kathir reads ayah 59 as flowing directly out of what precedes it. In ayat 57–58 the Prophet ﷺ is told to declare that the punishment his people impatiently demanded was not his to send: "I do not have what you are hastily seeking (the torment). The decision is only for Allah." Ibn Kathir explains this: the ruling of the matter rests with Allah — if He wills, He will punish them soon in response to their wish, and if He wills, He will give them respite, out of His great wisdom.

Ibn Kathir pauses here on the hadith in the Two Sahihs — the wording he cites is Muslim's — in which ʿAʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ whether he had encountered a day harder than the day of Uhud. He recalled the day of ʿAqabah, when he presented himself to Ibn ʿAbd Yalil bin ʿAbd Kulal and was not answered, and departed overwhelmed with severe sorrow until, at Qarn ath-Thaʿalib, he looked up to find a cloud shading him — and in it Jibril, announcing that Allah had sent the Angel of the Mountains to await his command. That angel greeted him and offered, if he wished, to let al-Akhshabayn — the two mountains to the north and south of Makkah — fall upon the very people who had rejected him. The Prophet ﷺ answered: "No, but I hope that Allah will let them generate offspring who will worship Allah Alone, and will worship none besides Him."

Ibn Kathir then asks how this hadith sits with ayah 58 — "If I had that which you are asking for impatiently (the torment), the matter would have been settled at once between you and I" — and answers, Allah knows best: the ayah means that had the torment the disbelievers themselves demanded been in the Prophet's ﷺ hand at the time, he would have sent it upon them as they asked. In the hadith, by contrast, the disbelievers had asked for no torment at all; rather, the angel offered him the choice of letting the two mountains close in on the disbelievers and crush them, and he did not wish it — he chose patience and asked for respite out of compassion for them, so that Allah might bring from them offspring who would associate nothing with Him in worship.

That is the doorway into our passage. Torment, respite, decree — none of it rests with any creature. So ayah 59 begins, with the emphasis on the pronoun: *and with Him* are the keys of the unseen.

## The keys of the unseen (ayah 59)

**The word itself.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *mafātiḥ* is a plural whose singular can be read two ways: *maftaḥ*, meaning treasure, or *miftāḥ*, meaning key. Some commentators therefore translate "treasures of the unseen," others "keys." The outcome, Maʿārif observes, is the same — whoever holds the keys to the treasures owns the treasures. He alone has the power to bring them into existence and make them manifest as and when He has determined, as another ayah says: "We have treasures of everything, but We send them down in a particular measure" (15:21). And Arabic word order does quiet work here: by placing *ʿindahu* ("with Him") first, the sentence signals restriction and exclusivity — the keys are with Him and with no one else — a hint that is then made explicit: "none knows them but He."

**What "the unseen" (al-ghayb) means.** Maʿārif, citing Tafsir Mazhari, defines al-ghayb in the Qur'an's terminology as two kinds of things: what has not yet come into existence at all — who will be born when and where, who will live how long, when and where the rain will fall, everything about Qiyamah — and what already exists but Allah has not disclosed to any creature, like the true state of the child in the womb. From this one sentence, Maʿārif concludes, two things stand proved: that Allah's knowledge and power are perfect and all-encompassing, and that this is His exclusive attribute which no created being can acquire.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites here the hadith recorded by al-Bukhari, from Salim bin ʿAbdullah from his father, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The keys of the Unseen are five and none except Allah knows them," then recited the ayah of Surah Luqman (31:34): with Allah alone is knowledge of the Hour; He sends down the rain; He knows what is in the wombs; no person knows what he will earn tomorrow; and no person knows in what land he will die.

## What the unseen is not

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān spends real effort clearing away a common confusion, because doubters point to weather forecasters, physicians, astrologers, and fetal imaging and ask: do people not know the "unseen" too? The answer is a careful distinction. Knowledge acquired through means and instruments is not *ʿilm al-ghayb* at all. The forecaster reads traces of rain whose substance already exists; that is observation, not the unseen — and it remains estimation, frequently wrong, whereas real knowledge is certitude. Astronomical calculation of an eclipse is genuine knowledge, but of the perceptible, "very much like announcing the news of planes and trains reaching airports and stations." As for astrology's claims to the future, Maʿārif is blunt: "the emergence of one truth out of a hundred lies is no knowledge." Even fetal imaging yields technical approximation, not certainty.

And when Allah Himself informs a prophet of some future event through *wahy* (revelation), or a righteous servant through *kashf* (illumination) and *ilham* (inspiration), that portion ceases to be ghayb — the Qur'an itself calls it *anbaʾ al-ghayb*, "reports of the Unseen" (11:49), not al-ghayb. So "none knows them but He" stands with no exemptions.

Here Maʿārif draws the creedal line with full seriousness. To take the knowledge of an angel or messenger to be all-encompassing amounts to giving a messenger of Allah the status of Allah Himself and declaring him His equal — which is shirk (associating partners with Allah) according to the Qur'an. Maʿārif points to the confession the mushriks — those who set up such partners — will make in Surah al-Shuʿaraʾ: "By Allah, we were in an error manifest when we held you as equals with the Lord of the Worlds." Carrying the point into its commentary on the next ayah, Maʿārif adds the balance: Allah did bless His Messengers, and above them all the Last of them ﷺ, with knowledge of many unseen matters, more than the knowledge of all angels and prophets — but no one's knowledge can ever equal Allah's. To claim otherwise would be the kind of excess the Christians committed in their reverence for their prophet, when they began to hold the prophet as equal to his Lord. This is shirk — may Allah keep us all protected from it.

## From the sea to the leaf to the buried grain

The rest of ayah 59 turns from the unseen to the seen — *ʿilm al-shahadah*, Allah's knowledge of everything that exists. Maʿārif explains that "the land and the sea" here stands for the whole universe with all its existents — the way one says "morning and evening" to mean all time, or "the East and the West" to mean the whole world.

Then the lens narrows, deliberately, to the smallest things. "Not a leaf falls, but He knows it." Ibn Kathir marvels: if He knows the movements of even inanimate things, what of the living — and what of mankind and jinn, upon whom the Divine laws rest? He pairs it with 40:19: "Allah knows the fraud of the eyes, and all that the breasts conceal." Maʿārif adds a beautiful observation on why the *fall* of the leaf is mentioned: the fall is perhaps indicative of the leaf's life cycle — its fall from the tree is the end of its growth, and its last condition is pointed out "as a mirror to the rest of its conditions." Allah knows how many times each leaf will swing and sway, when and where it will fall, and what circumstances it will pass through. Then deeper still: not a leaf falling in open sight, but a grain buried in the dark hollows of the earth; then wider: everything fresh and everything dry.

All of it, the ayah ends, is "in a Clear Record" (*kitab mubin*). The commentators differ over what this means: some say it is al-Lawh al-Mahfuz, the Preserved Tablet; others say it denotes Allah's own knowledge, called a "manifest book" because what is written stays preserved — nothing left to chance, mistake, or forgetting. Either way the point is the same: this knowledge is certain, not conjectural. Maʿārif gathers the parallel ayat — the mustard seed in a rock that Allah will bring forth (31:16), "not hidden from your Lord is (anything even) the weight of an atom in the earth or in the heaven" (10:61), "He knows what is before them and what is behind them. And they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills" (2:255), and "Allah encompasses all things in (His) Knowledge" (65:12).

## Your soul in His hand every night (ayah 60)

Ayah 60 moves from Allah's knowledge to His power, and it starts somewhere startlingly intimate: your sleep. "It is He, Who takes your souls by night (when you are asleep)." The verb is *yatawaffakum* — the very word the Qur'an uses for the taking of souls at death — and Ibn Kathir states it plainly: sleep is minor death. He cites 39:42: "It is Allah Who takes away the souls at the time of their death, and those that die not during their sleep. He keeps those (souls) for which He has ordained death and sends the rest for a term appointed" — both the minor and the major death in one ayah. Maʿārif notes that, according to hadith, sleep is similar to death in that it suspends the human body as death would.

"And has knowledge of all that you have done by day": your daytime deeds and actions, movements and idleness alike, lie as open to Him as your unconscious nights — "whether he be hid by night or go forth freely by day" (13:10). "Then He raises (wakes) you up again" — by day, as Mujahid, Qatadah and as-Suddi explained — "that a term appointed be fulfilled": the fixed life span of every person.

Maʿārif draws out the argument embedded in this daily rhythm. Every night you undergo a simulated death; every morning you personally witness a rising from it. The One who makes this happen to you daily can certainly bring about the collective death and collective rising called Qiyamah. Your own bed is the nightly proof of resurrection. Hence the ayah's ending: "Thereafter, to Him you are to return; then He will tell you what you have been doing" — the reckoning of deeds, then rewards and punishments.

## Guarded in life, gathered at death (ayah 61)

"He is al-Qahir over His servants." Ibn Kathir explains al-Qahir as the One who controls everything — all creation subservient to His supreme grace, greatness and majesty. And this irresistible power expresses itself, remarkably, first as protection: "He sends guardians (*hafazah*) over you" — angels appointed over mankind. Ibn Kathir shows their two functions from the Qur'an itself: they guard, "angels in succession, before and behind him. They guard him by the command of Allah" (13:11); and they watch and record, "But verily, over you (are appointed angels in charge of mankind) to watch you" (82:10) — "not a word does he utter, but there is a watcher by him, ready" (50:17–18).

Maʿārif adds the arresting turn: as long as Allah wills you alive, these angels protect you so that no one dares harm you — and when your appointed term arrives, *these very guardian angels become the agents of your death*. The protector and the collector are the same appointed servants of the same Master. "Our messengers take his soul" — Ibn ʿAbbas and several others explained that the Angel of Death has angels who pull the soul from the body, and when it reaches the throat, the Angel of Death captures it. "And they never neglect their duty": they guard the soul of the dead and take it wherever Allah wills — to ʿIlliyyin if righteous, to Sijjin if wicked; we seek refuge with Allah from that end.

Ibn Kathir here cites the hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad from Abu Hurayrah: the angels attend the dying person. To the righteous soul they say, "O pure soul from a pure body! Come out with honor and receive the good news of rest, satisfaction and a Lord Who is not angry," and it is raised up to heaven, welcomed at each asking of the door, until it reaches the heaven above which there is Allah. The wicked soul is ordered out in disgrace, given news of boiling and murky fluids, and finds the doors of heaven shut: "Return with disgrace" — and it is thrown back until it returns to the grave.

## Returned to the True Master (ayah 62)

"Then they are returned to Allah, their True Master (*mawlahum al-haqq*)." Ibn Kathir allows both readings of this return: the soul's return after death, as the hadith above describes, or the return of all creation on the Day of Resurrection, "so as to leave not one of them behind" (18:47).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān hears a deliberate mercy in the wording. If a person thinks only of standing before the greatest Judge of judges to account for a lifetime of deeds, he could not dare imagine escaping unscathed. So the ayah does not say they are returned merely to the Judge — it says to *their Master*: Allah is not only the Sovereign and Judge of judges, He is also the Master and Guardian of His servants who reaches out to help them at all times of their need. Justice and guardianship meet in the One you return to.

"Surely, His is the judgment" — His alone, and He is the best in His decision and decree. And to the mind that wonders how One alone could reckon the age-long deeds of billions: "He is the swiftest in taking account." Maʿārif's answer is that measuring what Allah does by the analogy of what human beings do is ignorance — He shall do it in no time at all.

## Living these ayat

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presents ayat 59–60 under the heading "the master prescription" for staying safe from sins, and names the discipline: *istihdar* — believing in these two attributes so strongly and completely that you begin to imagine them as present before you. A person who genuinely remains conscious that an All-Knowing, All-Powerful Master watches him in every word and deed, rest and movement — Who knows him outside in and inside out, and is aware of even the intention of the heart and the passing thought of the mind — cannot bring himself to take even a tiny step toward disobedience. These verses, Maʿārif concludes, are sovereign prescriptions that can make a person a model human being and correct, groom, and preserve his deeds and morals.

And the passage itself teaches you where to practice: at the falling leaf, which He knew; at night, when you hand Him your soul; at morning, when He returns it for the sake of a fixed term; and in the knowledge that the return at the end is not to a stranger, but to your True Master.

passages.title: Who rescues you from darkness on land and sea
passages.tafsir:
## One argument in three commands

These three ayat are a single, tightly-built argument, held together by three commands to the Prophet ﷺ — each ayah opens with *qul*, "Say". In ayah 63 he ﷺ is told to confront the Makkans with a question drawn from their own experience: who is it you actually call on when you are in mortal danger? In ayah 64 Allah Himself supplies the answer they cannot deny — it is Allah who rescues you, from that danger and from every distress — and then exposes the betrayal: *yet you commit shirk* (associating partners with Allah). And in ayah 65 the argument turns: the One who alone rescues is also the One who alone can punish — from above you, from beneath your feet, or from within your own ranks. Ibn Kathir gathers the whole passage under one heading: Allah's compassion and generosity, and His power and torment. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the thread from what came before: the previous verses described the perfection of Allah's Knowledge and Power; these verses now show manifestations of that very Knowledge and Power.

## The darknesses of land and sea (ayah 63)

The key word is **ẓulumāt** — a plural, "darknesses". Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that English has no plural for "darkness", but the Qur'anic plural is deliberate: darkness comes in many kinds — the darkness of night, of rain clouds, of dust storms, of the depths beneath the waves of the sea — and the plural sweeps all of them in. The scene the ayah paints is the Makkan traveller caught in catastrophe on a desert journey or a sea voyage. In that moment, Maʿārif observes, the idols are simply forgotten. Sometimes the travellers would confess their helplessness aloud; sometimes they would admit it only in their heart of hearts — that no one but Allah could save them from this. Hence the ayah's pairing *taḍarruʿan wa-khufyatan*: calling on Him "begging and in secret" — as Ibn Kathir puts it, in public and in secret. And with the plea comes the promise: *"If He only saves us from this, we shall truly be grateful."*

Ibn Kathir shows this is a repeated Qur'anic scene, citing 17:67 ("when harm strikes you at sea, those you call upon besides Him vanish from you except Him"), then 10:22 — the ship sailing with a fair wind until the storm closes in and the waves come from every side, and the passengers, certain they are encircled, call on Allah *making their faith pure for Him alone* — and 27:63 ("Is not He better Who guides you in the darkness of the land and the sea?"). In such moments, Ibn Kathir says, they call on Allah alone, without partners, in supplication.

## Allah Himself answers (ayah 64)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a fine observation about the structure here. The question of ayah 63 needed no reply — the Makkans could not deny that no idol had ever come to their aid in their hour of need. So in ayah 64 Allah takes the initiative and commands the Prophet ﷺ to declare the answer outright: *Allah rescues you from this* — and not only from the perils of travel, but *from every karb*, every distress and anxiety a person may face in life. Both rescue from danger and the removal of every hardship lie in Allah's hands alone — a truth even the most hardened disbelievers testified to under duress, when there was nothing else left to turn to.

Then the sting in the tail: *thumma antum tushrikūn* — "yet you commit shirk". Ibn Kathir explains: once back in comfort, they call on other gods besides Him. Maʿārif calls it what it is: "Strange betrayal and fatal ignorance indeed!"

## The One who rescues can also punish (ayah 65)

Ibn Kathir draws attention to where this warning sits: Allah says *"He has the power to send torment on you"* directly after His statement *"and yet you commit Shirk"* — and, as Ibn Kathir puts it, after He saves you. He then cites the parallel passage of Surah 17 (17:66–69): your Lord drives the ship for you through the sea; when harm strikes you at sea, all you call on besides Him vanishes; but when He brings you safely to land, you turn away — do you then feel secure that He will not cause a side of the land to swallow you up, or send you back to sea a second time and drown you?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out a subtle grammatical warning in the ayah itself: *ʿadhāban* ("a torment") is an indefinite noun carrying *tanwīn* (the "-an" ending marking indefiniteness), which in Arabic signals open-endedness — within the three directions named, the punishment could take many unspecified forms. He needs no police or army, as earthly rulers do; punishing is easy for Him.

Three directions are named:

**From above.** The commentators recall the flood upon the people of Nuh (peace be upon him), the windstorm that overtook ʿĀd, the stones rained on the people of Lut (peace be upon him), the blood and frogs upon Bani Isra'il, and the birds pelting the People of the Elephant who marched on Makkah.

**From beneath your feet.** The people of Nuh were caught between two punishments at once — the rainstorm from above and the waters forcing up from under the ground. The people of Pharaoh were drowned; Qarun (Korah) sank into the earth with his treasures.

Alongside this, Maʿārif records a second reading from the early authorities: Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid said the punishment from above is cruel rulers and merciless officials set over a people, and the punishment from beneath is one's own subordinates and servants turning into traitors, idlers and thieves. Maʿārif insists these explanations do not compete — the indefinite *ʿadhāban* embraces them all: stones, flood and the oppression of rulers are all "from above"; the earth swallowing its victims and the treachery of those under you are all "from beneath". And he cites prophetic teaching in support of Ibn ʿAbbas's reading — the narration in Mishkat (with reference to Shuʿab al-Iman of al-Baihaqi), "as are your deeds, so shall be your rulers set upon you", and the narration from ʿA'ishah in Abu Dawud and Nasa'i that when Allah wishes well for a ruler He gives him a good minister, and when evil is destined for a ruler, evil people are made his deputies. Sufyan al-Thawri put it with startling honesty: when a sin gets committed by me, I see its effect in my servant — even in my horse and my donkey; they start disobeying me. Such hardships, Maʿārif concludes, are no stray accidents but a punishment of one's deeds under a divine law — so trying to correct the situation through material ways and means alone is self-deception; the remedy is to examine one's deeds and leave disobedience, and then conditions will be commanded to change.

**From within: division.** The third punishment is *aw yalbisakum shiyaʿan*. Both commentaries linger on the language. Al-Bukhari glossed *yalbisakum* as "cover you with confusion — divide you into parties and sects"; Maʿārif traces it to the root *l-b-s*, "to hide or cover" (whence clothing, which covers the body, and *iltibās*, doubt and confusion, where meaning is hidden). *Shiyaʿ* is the plural of *shīʿah*, a band of partisans who rally round a cause — the Qur'an uses it of Ibrahim following in the footsteps of Nuh (37:83). So the third torment is a community shattered into factions, each wrapped in the confusion of its own cause — and its bitter fruit is the next clause: *"and make you taste the violence of one another"*, which Ibn ʿAbbas and others explained as torture and murder suffered at one another's hands. Al-Walibi reports from Ibn ʿAbbas that this ayah refers to *desires*; Mujahid and others said similarly.

## How the Prophet ﷺ received this ayah

The gravity of ayah 65 is measured by how the Prophet ﷺ himself responded to it. Jabir bin ʿAbdullah relates that when "Say: He has power to send torment on you from above" was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"I seek refuge with Your Face"*; at "or from under your feet" he ﷺ said again, *"I seek refuge with Your Face"*; but at "or cover you with confusion in party strife", he ﷺ said, *"This is less burdensome — or easier."* Al-Bukhari recorded this (including in the book of Tawhid of his Sahih), and An-Nasa'i in the book of Tafsir.

Then the passage's most sobering hadith. Saʿd bin Abi Waqqas relates that the Prophet ﷺ prayed two rakʿahs at the Masjid of Bani Muʿawiyah, supplicated long, and then said: *"I asked my Lord for three: I asked Him not to destroy my Ummah by drowning, and He gave that to me. I asked Him not to destroy my Ummah by famine, and He gave that to me. And I asked Him not to make them taste the violence of one another — but He did not give that to me."* Imam Ahmad recorded it, and Muslim recorded it in the book on Fitan (trials) of his Sahih. Khabbab bin Al-Aratt witnessed a whole night of the Prophet's ﷺ prayer until dawn and heard the same: two requests granted — that this Ummah not be destroyed as the nations before were, and that their enemies not prevail over them — and the third, that it not be covered with confusion in party strife, refused. Imam Ahmad recorded it; An-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban in his Sahih, and At-Tirmidhi also recorded it, At-Tirmidhi grading it "Hasan Sahih".

Maʿārif draws the conclusion: the annihilating punishments that erased earlier nations will not wipe out this Ummah — but one punishment remains standing over it in this world: its own infighting. That is why, when this ayah came down, the Prophet ﷺ warned the Muslims: "Do not renege after me, becoming like disbelievers striking at the necks of each other" (deduced by Ibn Abi Hatim from Zayd ibn Aslam, as in Mazhari). Ibn Kathir likewise cites the report, transmitted through various chains, that this Ummah will divide into seventy-three groups, all in the Fire except one.

## When difference is punishment — and when it is mercy

Because the third punishment is division, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to define which difference is meant. The blameworthy, punishing difference is of two kinds: difference in principles and beliefs, and difference driven by self-interest, desires and fancies — the kind that breeds slander, factionalism and bloodshed, and which the Qur'an elsewhere condemns: "Hold on to the cord of Allah, all of you, and be not divided" (3:103). Entirely distinct from this is the difference of opinion among qualified jurists (*ikhtilāf*) in subsidiary matters, conducted under the principles of the Qur'an, Sunnah and consensus, where every party intends only obedience to Allah. That difference, Maʿārif says — citing the narration in Al-Jamiʿ Al-Saghir, "the difference of my Ummah is mercy" — is a blessing, not a curse. His picture: a main road divided into lanes for buses, cars and pedestrians looks like division, but everyone is travelling in one direction to one destination, and the lanes are a mercy, not a fracture. The great Mujtahid Imams differed while honouring one another; none called another's way false. The disease is never the difference itself but what enters with dishonest motives: suspicion, name-calling, and finally the violence this ayah names as ʿadhāb.

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes the circle with a lesson he says should land on Muslims "with the rasp of a lash". The Makkan idolaters, for all their betrayal, at least remembered Allah in the storm. And us? In sickness we think of nothing but doctors; in flood, of nothing but rescue services. We do not bow to carved idols, but the material support systems we trust in can become "no less than idols for us" when they absorb the reliance that belongs to Allah. The balance he strikes is precise, and it is not a rejection of means: medicine, treatment and rescue equipment are not useless — they are Allah's own creations and blessings, and we should use them *as His blessings*. But He is the prime mover: unless He wills, fire cannot burn, water cannot extinguish, medicine cannot benefit. The believer's first resort in distress is therefore Allah Himself — turning to Him, seeking forgiveness for past sins, resolving to leave them — and then taking the means with gratitude rather than self-congratulation.

He adds a lens through which to read hardship itself: the Qur'an teaches that worldly hardships are generally the outcome of people's own deeds and a mild sampling of the punishment of the Hereafter — "We shall make them taste a lesser punishment, prior to the greater punishment, so that they may return" (32:21); "The hardship that reaches you is an outcome of your evil deeds, while many of them Allah forgives" (42:30). Seen this way, hardships are a mercy in disguise: a jolt to wake the heedless before something greater. Al-Baydawi added the necessary nuance: for the sinful, calamities are traces of sin; for those protected from sin, they are tests of patience that raise their ranks in Paradise.

The passage ends: *"See how variously We explain the ayat, so that they may understand"* — Ibn Kathir: made clear, plain and duly explained, so that Allah's ayat, proofs and evidences are comprehended. Across these three ayat the one truth has been turned over from every side — the rescue, the ingratitude, the warning — so that it may be understood.

passages.title: Turning away from those who mock the revelation
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah al-Anʿām 66–70: Turning Away from Those Who Mock the Revelation

This passage teaches the Prophet ﷺ — and every believer after him — how to carry the truth among people who reject and ridicule it. It moves in three steps. First, Allah defines the limits of the Prophet's ﷺ responsibility toward his own denying people (ayat 66–67). Then the believers are commanded to physically withdraw from any gathering where Allah's verses are being mocked (ayat 68–69). Finally, the mockers themselves are diagnosed — people deceived by the life of this world who took their religion as play and amusement — together with a picture of the Day on which no protector, no intercessor, and no ransom will save them (ayah 70). What holds the five ayat together is a single discipline: you are not responsible for making anyone believe, but you are entirely responsible for where you sit.

## "I am not responsible for your affairs" (66–67)

Ayah 66 opens with a grief that strikes close to home: *"But your people have denied it (the Qur'an) though it is the truth."* Ibn Kathir explains that "your people" means Quraysh, that what they denied was the Qur'an — the guidance and clear explanation the Prophet ﷺ brought them — and that it is the truth "beyond which there is no other truth." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the detail that sharpens the sting: the Prophet ﷺ was himself from that same tribe. The ones rejecting him were his own kin.

The reply he is taught is striking: *"Say: I am not responsible for your affairs"* — in the Arabic, *lastu ʿalaykum bi-wakīl*. Ibn Kathir explains this as "I have not been appointed a guardian or watcher over you." Ibn Kathir titles this whole section "The Invitation to the Truth is Guidance Without Coercion," and connects it to Allah's words elsewhere: *"And say: The truth is from your Lord. Then whosoever wills, let him believe, and whosoever wills, let him disbelieve"* (18:29). His duty is to convey the Message; theirs is to hear and obey. Those who follow him will acquire happiness in this life and the Hereafter; those who defy him will become miserable in this life and the Hereafter.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the conversational setting: those people kept asking about the precise time when the promised punishment would come, and the Prophet ﷺ is instructed to tell them that he has not been appointed to fix that time for them. Ayah 67 then supplies the principle: *"For every news there is a reality"* — or, in the translation given, *"Every destined matter has a set time to transpire."* Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn 'Abbas and others that this means the news will occur, "perhaps after a while," and he pairs it with *"And you shall certainly know the truth of it after a while"* (38:88) and *"(For) each and every matter there is a decree (from Allah)"* (13:38). So *"and you will come to know"* is, in Ibn Kathir's words, a warning and a promise that will surely occur. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, for everything there is a point of time as determined in Divine knowledge; it will come at its own time, and they will see for themselves what happens when it does.

## Wading into the verses: the word khawd (68)

Ayah 68 turns from the Prophet's ﷺ duty to the believers' conduct: *"And when you see those who engage in false conversation about Our verses (of the Qur'an) by mocking at them, stay away from them till they turn to another topic."*

The key word repays attention. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *yakhūḍūna* — translated there as "indulge" — comes from *khawḍ*, which basically means to enter into water and wade through it, and from there came to denote entering into activities that are vain, absurd, or futile.
