Allah sends rain \"in due measure, as a blessing and provision for the servants, relief and means of survival for the creatures, and mercy from Allah for His creation\" (Ibn Kathir) — and with it brings out vegetation of every kind, as He says elsewhere, *\"We have made from water every living thing\"* (21:30).

Then the verse moves in close, like a hand parting the leaves: green stalks — green produce and trees on which seeds and fruits grow; thick clustered grain, lined on top of each other in clusters like an ear or spike of grain; and from the sprouts of the date-palm, clusters *dāniyah* — \"hanging low,\" within reach and easy to pick. Ibn Kathir cites here the explanation ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah al-Wālibī related from Ibn ʿAbbās: the low-hanging clusters are the short date-trees whose branches hang low, close to the ground — a report recorded by Ibn Jarīr. Then gardens of grapes — Ibn Kathir remarks that grapes and dates were the most precious fruits to the people of the Hijaz, and perhaps the best fruits of this world — and olives and pomegranates, \"similar yet different\": leaves alike in shape and appearance, the fruit of each plant different in shape and taste, as Qatādah and several others explained.

Then a command: **unẓurū** — *\"Look at their fruits when they begin to bear, and at their ripening\"* (*yanʿih* means when the fruits become ripe, according to al-Barāʼ ibn ʿĀzib, Ibn ʿAbbās and others). Ibn Kathir spells out what the looking is for: contemplate the ability of the Creator who brought grapes and dates into existence out of what had been dry wood — the same power behind every colour, shape, taste and fragrance in creation, watering neighbouring plots *\"with the same water, yet some of them We make better than others to eat\"* (13:4).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a note on the passage's architecture. Three universes are toured here: the low world, the high world, and the atmosphere between them. The survey begins with the low, because it is closest to us — first vegetation, whose growth and flowering anyone can observe, then the deeper matter of ensouled life; it moves through the atmosphere's life-support of morning and evening; it rises to the sun, the moon and the stars; and then, because the low world is what we observe most, it returns there to conclude — briefly at first, now in loving detail, and in the detailed telling the order is reversed, the living recipients of blessing given precedence over the vegetation, since detail is where gratitude for blessings is expressed and the blessed deserve first mention there. Rain is threaded in between as the servant of vegetation — and rain uniquely belongs to all three realms: in origin it comes from the high, in destination it comes down to the low, and in the distance covered it is part of the atmosphere.

## Who sees the signs

Notice how each movement of the passage closes with a different audience. The stars are explained \"for people who **know**\" — those with sound minds, able to recognize the truth and avoid falsehood (Ibn Kathir, ayah 97). The two stations of the soul are detailed \"for people who **understand**\" — those who comprehend Allah's Words and their meanings (ayah 98). And the ripening fruit holds signs \"for people who **believe**\" — who believe in Allah and obey His Messengers (ayah 99). The signs themselves have been made *plain*; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes that whoever still fails to recognize Allah's presence and power from proofs this open is simply unaware and unconscious.

The passage's practical demand is its own single imperative: *look*. Treat the split seed, the broken dawn, the compulsory gift of sleep, the punctual moon and the low-hanging cluster of dates not as background scenery but as arguments — and then answer the question the passage opens with, *\"how then are you deluded?\"*, by refusing to give what belongs to the Creator to anything He created.

passages.title: Allah exalted above jinn partners and offspring
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah al-Anʿām 100–103 — Allah Exalted Above Every Partner and Every Offspring

This passage is the moment where Sūrah al-Anʿām turns from displaying Allah's creation to demolishing every false claim made about its Creator. The preceding verses have walked the reader through the whole created order — Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān notes how that section deliberately moves through three universes: the low (the earth with its vegetation and its life forms — beasts, human beings and animals), the high (the sun, the moon and the stars), and the atmosphere with its life-support system, the morning and the evening — a thematic order whose detailed telling, it observes, highlights the expression of gratitude for blessings. Now, in ayat 100–103, the Qurʼān confronts what people did with that evidence: they took the very creatures Allah made — jinn, and imagined sons and daughters — and set them up beside Him. The four ayat form a single argument that rises step by step: a rebuke of the false claims (100), a rational demolition of them (101), the conclusion that only Allah deserves worship (102), and a closing declaration of His transcendence — no vision can grasp Him, while nothing escapes His grasp (103).

## How Do Idol-Worshippers End Up Worshipping Jinn? (Ayah 100)

Ayah 100 says the idolaters "join the jinn as partners in worship with Allah, though He has created them." Ibn Kathir raises the obvious question: these people were only idol-worshippers — so in what sense did they worship *jinn*?

His answer is one of the most penetrating insights in this passage: **they worshipped the jinn by obeying them.** It was the jinn who commanded them to worship the idols, and in following that command against Allah, their obedience itself became worship. Worship, in other words, is not only bowing and sacrifice; it includes submitting your obedience to a creature in defiance of the Creator.

Ibn Kathir supports this from across the Qurʼān with a chain of ayat about Shayṭān: his vow to take "an appointed portion" of Allah's servants and mislead them (4:117–120); Allah's challenge, "Will you then take him (Iblis) and his offspring as protectors and helpers rather than Me?" (18:50); Ibrahim's plea to his father, "O my father! Worship not Shayṭān. Verily! Shayṭān has been a rebel against the Most Beneficent (Allah)" (19:44); Allah's ordinance to the Children of Adam that they should not worship Shayṭān, "a plain enemy to you," but worship Him — "that is a straight path" (36:60–61); and the scene on the Day of Resurrection when the angels will proclaim: "Glorified be You! You are our Protector instead of them. Nay, but they used to worship the jinn; most of them were believers in them" (34:41).

The ayah then adds a phrase that unravels the whole practice: *wa-khalaqahum* — "though He created them." The beings they elevated to partnership are themselves Allah's handiwork. Ibn Kathir presses the logic with Ibrahim's words to his people: "Worship you that which you (yourselves) carve? While Allah has created you and what you make!" (37:95–96). Allah alone is the Creator without partners; therefore He alone deserves to be worshipped without partners.

**The word *kharaqū*.** The second half of the ayah says they *kharaqū* for Him sons and daughters "without knowledge." According to the scholars of the Salaf, *kharaqū* means they *falsely attributed, invented, claimed and lied*. It is a word of fabrication: they did not discover something about Allah; they manufactured it. Ibn Kathir identifies the three fabrications in view: the Jews who claimed ʿUzayr as Allah's son, the Christians who claimed ʿIsa, and the Arab pagans who called the angels Allah's daughters. Against all of it stands the ayah's closing cry: *subḥānahu wa-taʿālā ʿammā yaṣifūn* — He is holier than, hallowed and exalted far above the sons, rivals, equals and partners that these ignorant, misled people attribute to Him.

## The Argument From Creation Itself (Ayah 101)

Ayah 101 does not merely deny the claim of offspring; it shows why the claim collapses under its own weight.

**Badīʿ — the Originator without precedence.** Allah is *Badīʿ al-samāwāti wa-l-arḍ*. Ibn Kathir explains, as Mujahid and as-Suddi said, that this means He originated, created, invented and brought the heavens and the earth into existence *without precedence*. He adds a linguistic note that makes the word unforgettable: the word for innovation — *bidʿah* — comes from this same root, because it names something that did not have a precedence.

**"How can He have a child when He has no wife?"** The ayah then asks a question designed to expose the absurdity of the fabrication on its own terms. A child, Ibn Kathir explains, is the offspring of two compatible spouses. But Allah has no equal; none of His creatures are similar to Him, for He alone created the entire creation. How could He have a wife from His own creation who is suitable for His majesty, when there is none like Him? And if no spouse is conceivable, no child is conceivable — verily, Allah is glorified above having a son. Ibn Kathir links this to the thunderous passage of Sūrah Maryam: "They say: 'The Most Beneficent (Allah) has begotten a son.' Indeed you have brought forth (said) a terrible evil thing" (19:88–89), running on to the verse: "And every one of them will come to Him alone on the Day of Resurrection" (19:95).

The ayah closes with the positive truth that replaces the fabrication: "He created all things, and He is the All-Knower of everything." Everything other than Allah is created by Him and known by Him through and through — which leaves nothing in existence fit to be His partner or His child.

## The Conclusion: "Such Is Allah, Your Lord" (Ayah 102)

Ayah 102 gathers the argument into its verdict. *Dhālikumu Allāhu rabbukum* — "Such is Allah, your Lord": the One who created everything and has neither son nor wife. Ibn Kathir spells out the consequence: none has the right to be worshipped but He, the Creator of all things — **so worship Him**, alone, without partners, attesting to His Oneness (*tawḥīd* — affirming that there is no deity worthy of worship except Him). He has neither descendants nor ascendants, neither wife, equal nor rival.

Notice the movement of the passage: ayat 100–101 clear the ground of false gods; ayah 102 builds on the cleared ground. The Qurʼān never leaves the reader with mere refutation — denial of the false partners flows directly into the command to worship the true Lord.

**Al-Wakīl — the Guardian over all things.** The ayah ends: *wa-huwa ʿalā kulli shayʼin wakīl*. Ibn Kathir unfolds *Wakīl* as Trustee, Watcher and Disposer of affairs for all things in existence — the One who gives them their provisions and their protection *by day and by night*. This is the practical heart of the passage for the believer: the Lord you are commanded to worship is not distant from what He made; He is continuously managing, sustaining and guarding it. Worship of Him and reliance upon Him belong together.

## "No Vision Can Grasp Him" (Ayah 103)

The passage closes with one of the great verses about Allah's transcendence: *lā tudrikuhu al-abṣāru wa-huwa yudriku al-abṣār* — "No vision can grasp Him, but His grasp is over all vision."

**In this life.** Masruq narrated that ʿAʼishah said: "Whoever claims that Muhammad ﷺ has seen his Lord, will have uttered a lie against Allah" — and she cited this very ayah as her evidence. Ibn Kathir also relays what is recorded in the Sahih (Muslim), narrated by Abu Musa al-Ashʿari from the Prophet ﷺ: "Verily, Allah does not sleep and it does not befit His majesty that He should sleep. He lowers the scale (of everything) and raises it. The deeds of the day are ascended to Him before the night, and the deeds of the night before the day. His Veil is the Light — or Fire — and if He removes it (the veil), the Light of His Face will burn every created thing that His sight reaches." Ibn Kathir adds that in the previous revealed Books there is this statement: when Musa requested to see Him, Allah said to Musa, "O Musa! Verily, no living thing sees Me, but it dies and no dried thing sees Me, but it rolls up" — and the Qurʼān itself records that when his Lord appeared to the mountain, He made it collapse to dust and Musa fell down unconscious (7:143). No created eye, in this world, can bear the sight.

**In the Hereafter.** Yet Ibn Kathir is emphatic that these ayat, hadiths and statements do not negate the fact that Allah *will* be seen on the Day of Resurrection by His believing servants, in the manner that He decides, all the while preserving His might and grace as they are. This, he says, is affirmed and attested to by the numerous hadiths from the Prophet ﷺ through authentic chains of narration in the collections of the Sahihs, Musnad and Sunan collections.

**How do the two truths fit together?** The verse's key word is rendered "grasp" — or, as it is also translated, "encompass": "No vision can *encompass* Him, but He *encompasses* all vision." ʿAʼishah, the Mother of the Faithful, used to affirm that Allah will be seen in the Hereafter while denying that it could occur in this life, citing this ayah as evidence — and Ibn Kathir explains that her denial was a denial of the ability to *encompass* Him: to perfectly see His grace and magnificence as He is, which is not possible for any human, any angel, or anything created. On this reading, what the ayah denies is the encompassing of Allah — not the believers' seeing of Him in the Hereafter. As-Suddi read the verse with this-worldly focus: "Nothing sees Him (in this life), but He sees all creation" — and Ibn Kathir records this reading alongside the other.

**"But His grasp is over all vision."** The second half reverses the direction completely. He encompasses all vision and has full knowledge of them, for He created them all — and Ibn Kathir notes it is also possible that "all vision" refers to those who have the vision. He connects this to "Should not He Who has created know? And He is the Most Subtle, Well-Acquainted (with all things)" (67:14). The asymmetry is the whole point of the passage: creatures cannot encompass the Creator, while nothing about the creatures lies outside His encompassment.

**Al-Laṭīf al-Khabīr.** The ayah seals the passage with two names. Abu al-ʿAliyah explained: He is *al-Laṭīf* — the Most Subtle, bringing forth all things — and *al-Khabīr* — Well-Acquainted with their position and place. Ibn Kathir illustrates with Luqman's advice to his son: even a deed the weight of a grain of mustard seed, though it be in a rock, or in the heavens or in the earth, Allah will bring it forth — "Verily, Allah is Most Subtle, Well-Acquainted" (31:16). Nothing is too small, too hidden or too interior for His knowledge.

## Living These Ayat

Two things follow directly from what the sources teach here. First, ayah 100 widens our understanding of *shirk* (associating partners with Allah): the pagans were only idol-worshippers, never bowing to a jinn directly — yet obeying the jinn's command to worship the idols counted as worshipping them. A believer therefore watches not only what he bows to, but *whom he obeys* when that obedience contradicts Allah. Second, the passage pairs transcendence with intimacy. The Lord whom no vision can grasp is, in the very same breath, al-Wakīl who gives all things their provisions and protection by day and night, and al-Laṭīf al-Khabīr from whom not even a mustard seed's weight is hidden. He is utterly beyond us — and nearer to our affairs than anything we can see. That combination — awe without distance — is exactly what the command of ayah 102 asks us to bring to Him: *so worship Him*.

passages.title: Insight has come; the Prophet compels no one
passages.tafsir:
This short passage defines, with complete clarity, what a Messenger is — and what he is not. Allah declares that the means of seeing the truth have already arrived; from that point on, whoever opens his eyes benefits only himself, and whoever shuts them harms only himself. The unit is held together by a single refrain at its two ends: ayah 104 closes with the Prophet ﷺ saying "I am not a keeper (ḥafīẓ) over you," and ayah 107 closes with Allah telling him "We have not made you a keeper over them." Between those two statements the Qur'an explains why the same clear signs produce opposite reactions in different hearts, and gives the Prophet ﷺ his own marching orders: follow the revelation, and leave the deniers to Allah.

## Baṣāʾir: sight for the heart

The key word of ayah 104 is **baṣāʾir**, the plural of *baṣīrah*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the distinction carefully: *baṣar* is physical vision, the eye's ability to see, while *baṣīrah* is insight — "the power through which one can acquire the knowledge of things which do not fall within the range of perception through the senses." Baṣāʾir here, the commentary says, means the evidences and sources through which one can get to know truth and reality.

What are these baṣāʾir concretely? Ibn Kathir says they are "the proofs and evidences in the Qur'an and the Message of Allah's Messenger ﷺ." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān spells the list out: the Qur'an has come, the Prophet ﷺ himself has come, his miracles were manifest, and his character, dealings and teachings were observed openly. All of these together are "means of seeing the truth."

Then comes the grammar of responsibility. "Whoever sees, it is *for* himself (fa-li-nafsihi); whoever is blind, it is *against* himself (fa-ʿalayhā)." Ibn Kathir pairs this with the same construction elsewhere: "Whosoever receives guidance, he does so for the good of himself, and whosoever goes astray, he does so at his own loss" (10:108). And he identifies which blindness is meant by quoting 22:46 — "it is not the eyes that grow blind, but it is the hearts which are in the breasts that grow blind." The one who refuses these baṣāʾir is not deprived of evidence; he has closed the organ that receives it. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, whoever has used these means becomes the one blessed with true insight, his benefits secured, while the one who elected to remain blind to the truth by ignoring them ends up losing what was good.

## "I am not a keeper over you"

The ayah ends: *wa-mā ana ʿalaykum bi-ḥafīẓ* — "I am not a ḥafīẓ over you." A ḥafīẓ is a guardian or watcher, someone stationed over people to police them. Ibn Kathir explains: the Prophet ﷺ is "neither responsible, nor a watcher over you. Rather, I only convey; Allah guides whom He wills and misguides whom He wills." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point in institutional terms: the Prophet ﷺ was never given the job of *forcing* people to stop doing wrong, the way an appointed overseer does — or, as the commentary pointedly adds, the way self-appointed vigilantes do in our own day. "The functional responsibility of a messenger of Allah is only to convey commands, and explain. After that, following or not following the message conveyed becomes a matter of personal discretion and responsibility of the addressees."

Ayah 107 completes the thought with a second word: the Prophet ﷺ is not a ḥafīẓ over them, "nor are you a **wakīl** over them" — not a trustee set over their affairs. Ibn Kathir glosses: not a watcher who observes their statements and deeds, and not one who disposes of their affairs or controls their provision. He anchors this in two parallel verses: "So remind them; you are only one who reminds. You are not a dictator over them" (88:21–22), and "Your duty is only to convey, and on Us is the reckoning" (13:40). Conveying belongs to the Prophet ﷺ; the accounting belongs to Allah alone.

## One revelation, two responses (ayah 105)

Ayah 105 turns to the signs themselves: "Thus We explain variously the verses (*nuṣarrifu al-āyāt*)…" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān connects this back to everything the sūrah has just done — argument after argument for tawḥīd (Allah's oneness) and for the truth of prophethood, presented from different angles. Ibn Kathir adds that this varied exposition is deliberate: Allah makes the āyāt (the verses and signs) "plain and clear in all circumstances, to suffice the ignorance of the ignorant."

Then comes the startling clause: the signs are varied "so that they say, *darasta* — 'you have studied.'" Ibn Kathir explains the taunt: the idolaters and disbelievers who denied the Prophet ﷺ would say, "O Muhammad! You have studied with those who were before you from among the People of the Book and learned with them." He reports that Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Saʿīd bin Jubayr and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk explained it this way, and he cites aṭ-Ṭabarānī's narration from ʿAmr bin Kaysān that he heard Ibn ʿAbbās say that *darasta* means "recited, argued and debated." Ibn Kathir sets it beside the same slander elsewhere: "This is nothing but a lie that he has invented, and others have helped him at it… tales of the ancients, which he has written down, and they are dictated to him morning and afternoon" (25:4–5); and beside al-Walīd bin al-Mughīrah al-Makhzūmī, the "chief liar of the disbelievers," who thought and plotted and finally pronounced, "This is nothing but the word of a human being" (74:18–25).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān exposes how perverse the accusation was. Here was a total *ummiyy* — a man who had never been schooled or tutored by anyone — "expressing with inimitable eloquence volumes of knowledge and reality," bringing a Book whose challenge to produce even one small sūrah stands unanswered by all jinn and mankind until the end of time. Such was the class and substance of this treasure trove of truth, the commentary says, that even the most diehard denier should have fallen at the blessed feet of the Prophet ﷺ. Instead, "people who were chronically crooked in their ways" reached for "you have been tutored."

So the ayah names both outcomes in one breath: the same varied signs end with the deniers saying *darasta*, "and that We may make the matter clear for the people who have knowledge." Ibn Kathir draws out the principle: the āyah means Allah explains the matter "to a people who know truth, and thus follow it, and know falsehood, and thus avoid it. Allah's wisdom is perfect, He allows the disbelievers to stray, and He guides the people who have knowledge." He then assembles a whole family of verses making the same point — "By it He misleads many, and many He guides thereby" (2:26); the Qur'an is "a healing and a mercy to the believers, and it increases the wrongdoers in nothing but loss" (17:82); "It is for those who believe a guide and a healing. And as for those who disbelieve, there is heaviness in their ears, and it is blindness for them" (41:44) — and he closes the survey by noting that similar āyāt testify that Allah sent down the Qur'an as guidance to those who fear Him, and that He guides or misguides whom He wills by the Qur'an. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, the sources of guidance were placed before everyone — the crooked took no advantage of the opportunity, while the wise owned them heartily "and became the leaders of their world."

## The Prophet's own course (ayat 106–107)

Having freed the Prophet ﷺ of responsibility for results, Allah gives him his actual task in ayah 106: "Follow what has been revealed to you from your Lord — there is no deity worthy of worship but He — and turn aside from the idolators." Ibn Kathir notes that this command embraces the Prophet ﷺ and everyone who follows his path: follow the revelation, obey it, act on it, for it is the truth without doubt. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the Prophet ﷺ is here being asked not to worry about the acceptance or non-acceptance of the call. His best course is to keep to the way revealed to him through waḥy (revelation), whose central element is that no one is worthy of worship but Allah — and continuing to preach that message of truth is itself part of what was revealed.

"Turn aside from the idolators" is not contempt. Ibn Kathir's gloss is remarkably gentle: it means "forgive them, be forbearing and endure their harm until Allah brings relief to you, supports you and makes you triumphant over them." The turning aside is patience with a promise attached.

Then ayah 107 answers the unspoken question — *why does the denial continue at all?* — with a statement about divine will: "Had Allah willed, they would not have associated others with Him." Ibn Kathir words it as an address to the Prophet ﷺ: know that "there is a wisdom behind misleading the idolators," and that had Allah willed, He would have directed all people to guidance. "Allah's is the perfect will and wisdom in all decrees and decisions, and He is never questioned about what He does, while they all will be questioned." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unfolds the same balance: had Allah willed, by His creational decree, that the whole human race be Muslim, shirk (associating partners with Allah) would have been impossible. But because of their own misdeeds, Allah willed that they be punished and created the conditions leading to that end. Notice how both commentators hold the two truths together: nothing happens outside Allah's will — He guides whom He wills and misguides whom He wills — and yet the deniers stray "because of their misdeeds" and will be questioned for them. Divine will does not cancel human responsibility; the passage affirms both without dissolving either.

And so the unit closes where it began: "We have not made you a ḥafīẓ over them, nor are you a wakīl over them." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the comfort out plainly: the Prophet ﷺ should feel no anxiety over what the deniers choose to do with their own souls. He was not made to stand guard over them, nor authorized to bring punishment upon them.

## Living it

One command in this passage explicitly reaches beyond the Prophet ﷺ: Ibn Kathir tells us that "Follow what has been revealed to you" addresses Allah's Messenger ﷺ *and those who follow his path*. That much is every believer's share — follow the revelation, obey it, act on it. The rest of the passage describes the Messenger's own office, and in describing it, teaches every reader how guidance works. The means of seeing the truth have already arrived, and the outcome is written into the grammar: whoever sees, sees for his own good; whoever chooses blindness harms only himself. Even the Messenger ﷺ, with manifest miracles and the inimitable Qur'an in hand, was made a conveyer and an explainer — not a ḥafīẓ, not a wakīl — and the response remained "a matter of personal discretion and responsibility of the addressees." And even that clearest of evidence was still answered with "darasta": ayah 105 says the same varied exposition that leaves one people reaching for a rationalization makes the matter clear to a people who know. The final accounting of every soul rests with Allah alone — "Your duty is only to convey, and on Us is the reckoning."

passages.title: Do not insult the idols of others
passages.tafsir:
This single ayah lays down one of the most striking commands in the Qur'an: believers are forbidden to insult the false gods of the idolaters — not because those idols deserve respect, but because insulting them would provoke the idolaters into insulting Allah Himself. In one verse, the Qur'an teaches that a Muslim is responsible not only for his own act, but for what his act predictably causes others to do.

## The story behind the verse

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates the background of revelation as narrated by Ibn Jarir. When Abu Talib, the Prophet's ﷺ beloved uncle and protector, lay on his deathbed, the chiefs of Quraysh grew alarmed. They had long plotted against the Prophet ﷺ, but killing him after his uncle's death would disgrace them — people would say they dared act only once his protector was gone. So a deputation was formed — Abu Sufyan, Abu Jahl, ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀs and others — and they went to Abu Talib with a proposal: tell your nephew to say nothing offensive against our idols, and we will make peace; let him worship whom he chooses, and we will raise no objection.

Abu Talib called the Prophet ﷺ, who turned to the deputation and asked what they wished. When they laid out their offer, he replied with a counter-offer: would they be willing to say one *Kalimah* — a single statement — by which they would become masters of all Arabia, with peoples beyond it submitting to their authority? Abu Jahl said they were ready to say ten. The Prophet ﷺ said: **لا إله إلا الله** — *there is no god worthy of worship but Allah.* The chiefs were infuriated. Abu Talib urged his nephew to say something else, for this Kalimah had left his clansmen confounded. He answered: "As for me, I cannot say a Kalimah other than this. If they were to bring the sun down from the skies and put it in my hands, even then I will not say a Kalimah other than this."

Still in anger, the chiefs issued their ultimatum: either you stop speaking ill of our idols, or we will start insulting you — and the very Being whose messenger you claim to be. It was then that this verse came down.

Ibn Kathir records the same essence from the early authorities: ʿAli bin Abi Talhah reports Ibn ʿAbbas saying that the disbelievers threatened, "O Muhammad! You will stop insulting our gods, or we will insult your Lord" — whereupon Allah prohibited the believers from insulting their idols. And Qatadah (as narrated by Abdur-Razzaq from Maʿmar) said: "Muslims used to insult the idols of the disbelievers and the disbelievers would retaliate by insulting Allah wrongfully without knowledge," and so the verse was revealed.

## The word, and who is being addressed

The verb *lā tasubbū* ("do not insult") comes from *sabb* — to abuse someone, to hurl insulting language at them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes a beautiful subtlety in the grammar. In the two verses immediately before this one (106–107), the address is to the Prophet ﷺ alone, in the singular: *follow what has been revealed to you*, *turn away from the idolaters*, *We have not made you a guard over them*. Then, at this verse, the address suddenly turns plural: *lā tasubbū* — addressed to the Muslims in general. Why the switch? Because the Prophet ﷺ had never in his life used abusive speech against anyone — not even in childhood, not even toward an animal. To address the prohibition to him directly could have disheartened him, as though he were suspected of it. So the command was made general — and, as noted in Al-Bahr Al-Muhīt, all the Companions began taking precaution in this matter. Perhaps some hard word had escaped the lips of a Companion which the Makkans overestimated as an insult and seized upon as their pretext; the verse closed that door for the whole community.

## Why forbid what seems justified?

Ibn Kathir states the logic plainly: there is a clear benefit in denouncing false deities — yet insulting them here would lead to a greater evil than its benefit, for the idolaters might retaliate by insulting Allah, "none has the right to be worshipped but He." The Qur'an's own words capture the imbalance: they would insult Allah *ʿadwan bi-ghayri ʿilm* — "wrongfully, without knowledge." The believer who provokes that blasphemy becomes its cause.

On this same principle — abandoning something beneficial to avert a greater evil — Ibn Kathir cites what is recorded in the Sahih, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Cursed is he who insults his own parents!" The Companions asked, "O Allah's Messenger! And how would a man insult his own parents?" He said: "He insults a man's father, and that man insults his father; and he insults his mother, and that man insults his mother." The man never uttered a word against his own parents — but he set the exchange in motion, so the sin traces back to him. This ayah applies exactly that logic at the highest level: do not become the channel through which Allah's name is reviled.

## But doesn't the Qur'an itself condemn idols?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious question: the Qur'an speaks of idols in strong words in several verses — "Weak are the seekers and weak the sought" (22:73); "You, and what you worship other than Allah, are but fuel for Hell" (21:98) — and those verses are not abrogated. Is that not insult?

The answer is a distinction any thoughtful speaker recognises: those verses are argument, not abuse. They expose the helplessness of idols — devoid of sense, knowledge, and power — in order to unfold reality for the understanding, the way a court examines a person's shortcomings to settle a case, or a physician describes defects for the sake of diagnosis. The intent is to state the sad end of error, not to wound or mock. And the jurists (as cited from Rūḥ al-Maʿānī) pressed the distinction to its logical end: if a Muslim were to recite even these Qur'anic verses *as a tool to irritate the disbelievers*, that recitation, at that time and for that purpose, would itself fall under the prohibited "insulting" and be impermissible. What matters is not only the words but the intent and effect.

## "Thus We made fair seeming to each people its own doings"

The ayah then explains why the idolaters would react so fiercely: *"Thus We have made fair seeming to each people its own doings."* Ibn Kathir comments: just as Allah made the idolaters' love of their idols and their zeal to defend them appear beautiful to them, so had the misguidance of every previous nation been made to seem fair in its own eyes — and Allah's is the most perfect proof and the most complete wisdom in all that He wills and chooses. This is realism about human nature: people are attached to what they venerate, however false, and will lash out to defend it. The verse does not ask the believer to pretend falsehood is true; it asks him to reckon with how people actually respond.

And it closes with the final court: *"then to their Lord is their return, and He shall inform them of all that they used to do"* — He will compensate every deed, good for good and evil for evil. The believer can leave the idols' fate to Allah; the reckoning is not his to force in the street.

## The principle the scholars drew out — and its limit

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws from this verse a principle from which, it says, the jurists deduced solutions to thousands of problems: **an act that is permissible in itself — even praiseworthy — becomes prohibited when doing it will necessarily bring about evil or lead people into sin.** Denouncing idols is at least permissible, perhaps even reward-worthy as a defence of one's faith; yet because it would cause people to speak ill of Allah, it was forbidden.

The Prophet ﷺ himself lived this principle. He told Sayyidah ʿA'ishah that the Kaʿbah, rebuilt by Quraysh before his prophethood, no longer stood on the original foundations of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) — the Hatim had been left out for lack of funds, the western door closed, the remaining door raised above the ground so that entry depended on Quraysh's permission. He said he wished to demolish the structure and rebuild it exactly on Ibrahim's foundations — but the danger was that the common Arabs, so newly entered into Islam, might fall into doubt at the sight of the Kaʿbah being torn down. So he abandoned the intention. Rebuilding the House on its true foundations would have been an act of obedience and merit — yet he set it aside to protect weaker hearts.

But the principle has a crucial limit, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the objection reported from Abu Mansur in Rūḥ al-Maʿānī: if we abandon everything that provokes evil, must we abandon jihad, the propagation of Islam, the recitation of the Qur'an, the Adhan and the Salah — all of which disbelievers mock? Abu Mansur's answer supplies the missing condition: **the act abandoned must not itself be one of the basic objectives and necessary duties of Islam.** Insulting idols serves no Islamic objective; neither does the precise architecture of the Kaʿbah. But acts that *are* the objectives of the religion — or on which such objectives depend — are never surrendered because of others' wrongdoing; instead, effort is made to continue them while blocking the evil as far as possible. The very story of this verse's revelation proves it: the same Prophet ﷺ who accepted the ban on insulting idols refused, even for the sun placed in his hands, to stop proclaiming that Allah is One. What was negotiable was the insult; the message never was.

A story from the early generations makes the same point. Hasan al-Basri and Ibn Sirin (may Allah have mercy on them) once went out for a funeral prayer and found men and women mixed in the gathering. Ibn Sirin turned back. But Hasan al-Basri said: why should we abandon what is necessary because of other people's false practice? The Janazah prayer is *fard* — obligatory — and cannot be abandoned because of a corrupting circumstance; rather, one strives to root out the evil itself. (Reported in Rūḥ al-Maʿānī.)

## Living it

The jurists applied this verse to daily life in ways that may surprise you. A father with a defiant son, who knows a direct order will only be met with refusal — loading the boy with the sin of fresh disobedience — should frame his wish as gentle counsel instead: "if such-and-such could be done, that would be nice" (Khulāsatul-Fatāwā). Likewise with advice generally: if the signs show a person will react to your counsel by sinking deeper into sin, holding back is better. Imam al-Bukhari devoted a chapter of his Sahih to this very subject — leaving certain preferred things for fear that some people's understanding will fall short and they will fall into something worse.

The working rule, then, as the passage sums it up: what is permissible but not a binding religious objective is given up when it will predictably produce evil — indeed giving it up becomes *wajib* (necessary); what is a core objective of the religion is never given up, though every effort is made to contain the harm. This ayah asks the believer for a particular kind of discipline: to measure words not only by whether they are true, but by what they will set in motion — and to care more for the honour of Allah's name than for the satisfaction of scoring a point.

passages.title: Their oaths for signs and the devilish enemies
passages.tafsir:
This passage answers a challenge the Quraysh threw at the Prophet ﷺ: *show us one spectacular miracle of our choosing and we swear by Allah we will believe.* Ayah 109 records their oath and Allah's reply; ayat 110–111 expose why no miracle — not even angels descending or the dead speaking — would have moved them; and ayat 112–113 turn to console the Prophet ﷺ himself: this hostility is nothing new, for every prophet before him faced enemies, devils of mankind and jinn whispering polished falsehood to one another. What holds the five ayat together is a single diagnosis: their unbelief was never a problem of evidence. It was a disease of the heart — and a heart set on rejection cannot be cured by miracles.

## The mountain of gold

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān, citing a report of Ibn Jarir, gives the occasion that unlocks ayah 109. The chiefs of Quraysh came with a demand: let the Mount of Ṣafā be turned into solid gold, and they would accept Muhammad ﷺ as a prophet and messenger and embrace Islam. The Prophet ﷺ took them at their word: *make a solid agreement, then — if this miracle is shown, all of you become Muslims.* They swore their solemn oaths. He stood up to pray that Allah turn the Mount into gold.

Then Jibrīl (peace be upon him) came with wahy — revelation — which said: **"If you wish, We shall make this whole Mount a Mount of gold"** — but know the consequence. By Allah's customary law, a people who demand a miracle, receive it, and still refuse to believe are destroyed through a mass punishment. It had happened with past communities who demanded a miracle which was shown, yet reverted to denial, and the wrath and punishment of Allah overtook them.

The Prophet ﷺ was aware of his people's habitual obstinacy. And because he was, in mercy, the foremost, he said he would not pray for that miracle anymore. Thereupon, ayah 109 was revealed.

## "Signs are only with Allah"

The disbelievers swore *jahda aymānihim* — their most strenuous, most solemn oaths. Allah's answer is one compressed sentence: **"Signs are but with Allah"** (ayah 109). Ibn Kathir explains: say to those who ask for signs out of defiance, disbelief and rebellion, not out of any desire for guidance and knowledge — the matter of sending signs is for Allah. If He wills He sends them; if He wills He ignores the request.

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān adds a second layer: the demand itself was illegitimate. The Prophet ﷺ claimed to be a Messenger of Allah and had already presented proofs and evidences in the form of miracles. The honest response to a claim backed by evidence is to examine that evidence and, if you can, refute it. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān puts it in courtroom terms: imagine a respondent who refuses to cross-examine the witnesses actually presented, and instead pleads that he will only accept testimony from some other witness of his own choosing. No court would consider such a plea worth hearing. Until the disbelievers could show the existing miracles to be false, they had no right to dictate which new miracle would satisfy them. The demand for a sign of one's own choosing is not inquiry; it is evasion dressed as inquiry.

Then comes a searching question: **"And what will make you perceive that even if it came, they would not believe?"** Ibn Kathir records two readings of who "you" addresses. According to Mujahid, it addresses the idolators themselves: what makes *you* perceive that you are truthful in these vows you have sworn? — meaning, even if the sign you demanded arrived, you still would not believe. The other view is that it addresses the believers: what makes *you* perceive, O believers who wish so eagerly for these people to believe, that if the signs came to them they would believe? On either reading the verdict is the same: the sign would have changed nothing.

## "We turn their hearts and their eyes" — ayah 110

This is the passage's most sobering sentence, and the early authorities Ibn Kathir gathers open it up carefully. Al-ʿAwfi reports from Ibn ʿAbbas: when the idolators rejected what Allah sent down, their hearts could no longer settle on any one thing; they turned away from every matter of benefit. Mujahid — and similarly ʿIkrimah and ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam — explained it as: We prevent them from faith, and even if every sign came, they would not believe, *just as We prevented them the first time*.

Notice the justice built into the wording: **"as they refused to believe therein for the first time."** The turning of their hearts is not arbitrary. It answers their own first refusal. They chose rejection when the truth first reached them clean and clear; Allah then dealt with them according to that choice. Ibn Kathir records, through ʿAli bin Abi Talhah, Ibn ʿAbbas's principle: Allah mentions what the servants will say before they say it and what they will do before they do it. In corroboration he cites the ayah, "And none can inform you like Him Who is the All-Knower" [35:14], and links the whole discussion to Surah al-Anʿam itself, ayah 28 — the disbelievers will beg to be sent back, yet "if they were returned, they would certainly revert to that which they were forbidden. And indeed they are liars." So the meaning of ayah 110, as Ibn Kathir draws it out, becomes: if they were sent back to this life, they would be prevented from embracing the guidance, just as they were prevented from it the first time, in the life of this world.

The ayah ends: **"and We leave them in their ṭughyān, wandering blindly."** *Ṭughyān* — trespass — means their disbelief according to Ibn ʿAbbas and as-Suddi, their misguidance according to Abu al-ʿAliyah, ar-Rabiʿ bin Anas and Qatadah. And *yaʿmahūn*: they wander blindly — or "playfully," in al-Aʿmash's gloss — wandering on in their disbelief, as Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Abu al-ʿAliyah, ar-Rabiʿ, Abu Malik and others commented, abandoned to the path they insisted upon.

## Even if angels came down — ayah 111

Ayah 111 closes the file on the evidence question with a deliberately extreme scenario. Suppose Allah granted everything they ever demanded: angels sent down to them — as they had asked, "or you bring Allah and the angels before us face to face" (Ibn Kathir cites 17:92 and 25:21) — the dead made to speak and inform them of the truth of what the Messengers brought, and all things gathered before their very eyes (the reading reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, and the view of Qatadah and ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd, as Ibn Kathir relays). Even then: **"they would not believe — unless Allah willed."**

The lesson, as Ibn Kathir draws it, is that guidance is with Allah, not with the signs. He guides whom He wills and misguides whom He wills, and He does what He wills — "He cannot be questioned about what He does, while they will be questioned" (21:23) — by His knowledge, wisdom, power, and supreme authority. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān states the underlying reason plainly: their denial never arose from misunderstanding or lack of awareness. It arose from hostility and obstinacy — "a disease which cannot be treated by miracles." Miracles address doubt; they cannot address a will that has already decided. Hence the ayah's closing verdict: "but most of them behave ignorantly" — swearing grand oaths about a faith they would not accept even if every demand were met.

## Every prophet has enemies — ayat 112–113

With the disbelievers' case closed, the passage turns tenderly to the Prophet ﷺ. Their hostility wounded him; these two ayat are his consolation. Ibn Kathir paraphrases: just as We made enemies for you, O Muhammad ﷺ, We made enemies for every Prophet before you — so do not be saddened. He gathers the parallel ayat: "Messengers were denied before you, but with patience they bore the denial, and they were hurt" (6:34); "Nothing is said to you except what was said to the Messengers before you" (41:43). And he recalls the words of Waraqah bin Nawfal to Allah's Messenger ﷺ: none ever came with what you have come with except that he was met with enmity. Opposition is not a mark against a prophet; it is part of the pattern of prophethood.

The enemies are named: **shayāṭīn al-ins wal-jinn** — devils of mankind and devils of the jinn. Ibn Kathir notes that the word *shayṭān* (devil) describes one who has become unlike his own kind through sheer wickedness — so a human being can be a shayṭān just as a jinn can. Qatadah (as ʿAbdur-Razzaq narrates from Maʿmar) said: there are devils among the jinn and devils among mankind, and they inspire one another. Their method is **zukhruf al-qawl** — adorned, gilded speech, beautified falsehood "as a delusion," inspired from one to another to deceive the ignorant who hear it. Evil rarely presents itself ugly; it comes polished.

Then a clause of pure creed: **"If your Lord had so willed, they would not have done it."** All of this — that every prophet has such enemies — occurs by Allah's decree, will, and decision, as Ibn Kathir affirms. Nothing in the opposition to truth escapes His control. And so the command: "leave them alone with their fabrications" — an order, Ibn Kathir says, of patience in the face of the harm of the wicked and of trust in Allah against their enmity, for Allah shall suffice His Messenger ﷺ and aid him against them.

Ayah 113 traces where the adorned speech lands. **"So that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may taṣghā to it"** — *taṣghā*, in Ibn ʿAbbas's gloss, means *incline*: lean toward it. Only those who disbelieve in the Hereafter accept this evil speech, as Ibn Kathir observes; such hearts incline to it, then **"remain pleased with it"** — they like it, adore it — and then **"commit what they are committing."** Ibn ʿAbbas (through ʿAli bin Abi Talhah) read this last clause as *let them earn whatever they will earn* — echoed by as-Suddi and Ibn Zayd: let them do whatever they will do. The wording echoes ayah 110's "We leave them in their trespass": those who choose deceit are left to it, and to what they earn by it.

## What this asks of a believer

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān draws the practical thread out of these ayat for the Muslim community directly. Our duty is twofold: hold firmly to the true faith ourselves, and convey it to others correctly and properly. That is where the duty ends. If people then persist in rigidity and obstinacy, we are not to agonize over them — no one is to be forced into Islam. And here Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān offers its most liberating point: if faith could rightly be produced by overwhelming force, who has greater power than Allah? He Himself would simply have made everyone a Muslim.

For anyone who calls to Allah — a parent, a teacher, a friend — this passage is a mercy. When sincere effort meets a wall, the fault does not necessarily lie in the evidence or the presenter. Some hearts have inclined elsewhere, and no accumulation of proofs will move them until the heart itself turns. Present the truth well, refuse to be baited by demands designed only to evade it, do not grieve beyond your duty, and leave the results with the One with whom all signs — and all guidance — rest.
